title: Fix ownership and demand planning before any hire or leadership training
hypothesis: If we name an owner for every operating artefact and fix demand planning before running leadership or team health work, then stockouts and missed peaks drop first, because an unowned process or a bad forecast costs more cash than low morale does.
does_not_apply_when: the store has already named an owner and cadence for every artefact and has a working forecast process

signal.check: No single name is written next to the tech pack, critical path, PO tracker, forecast, 3PL SLA, CS routing or scoreboard, or the team is booking leadership workshops before these exist.

expected_effect.size: no number given; the source claims stockouts and missed peaks stop first, not a percent

risk.note: Reordering the work plan costs nothing directly; the risk is delaying a leadership fix the team wants.

steps: List every operating artefact: tech pack, critical path, PO tracker, forecast sheet, 3PL SLA, CS routing rules, scoreboard.
Write 1 name and 1 update cadence next to each artefact.
Check demand planning and inventory ownership before the next peak or launch.
Check whether current people are underused before opening a new hire.
Diagnose the growth bottleneck, traffic vs conversion, before funding a hire or a CRO project.
Only after the steps above, schedule leadership or team health practice.

test.method: Not a lab test; a work order rule for the operations agenda.
test.measure: Whether ownership and planning gaps close before a hire or workshop is booked
test.read_point: Next planning cycle, or the next time a hire or workshop is proposed

title: Name 1 owner for each of the 5 core store silos before the first hire
hypothesis: If we write 1 name next to administrator, customer service, fulfilment, marketing and web work, even when every name is the founder, then a launch or a campaign stops stalling on an unowned task because nobody can say who was supposed to act.

signal.check: Nobody can say who owns returns, PDP copy, or the ad account when asked.

expected_effect.size: unknown; source gives no number, only that a blank silo is a launch blocker

risk.note: A naming exercise only; no operational change yet.

steps: List the 5 silos: administrator, customer service, order fulfilment, digital marketing, web development and design.
Write 1 name next to each, founder allowed for every one.
For a marketplace channel or subscription programme, add a separate named owner (see marketplace and subscription ideas).
Check monthly that no silo has gone dark for a month.

test.method: Checklist review, not a split test.
test.measure: Every silo has 1 name
test.read_point: Before the next launch or campaign, then monthly

title: Below about $1M revenue, have the founder run every silo and buy discrete tasks from freelancers
hypothesis: If the founder keeps running every operational silo below about $1M revenue and buys single tasks like a tech pack from freelancers instead of hiring 1 generalist, then payroll stays low while volume is still small, because 1 half-covering generalist does no silo well.
does_not_apply_when: revenue is already well past $1M and a silo has gone dark for a month

signal.check: Revenue is under about $1M and the team is discussing a first generalist hire to cover several silos at once.

expected_effect.size: no number given; 2 single-operator sources agree on the approach, not a saved amount

risk.note: Founder overload if a silo goes dark for a month; watch for that signal and hire then.

steps: Confirm current revenue is below about $1M.
List which silo tasks the founder currently drops or delays.
For any dropped task that is a discrete deliverable, such as a tech pack or a shoot, hire a freelancer for that task only.
Do not hire 1 generalist to half-cover all 5 silos.
Re-check monthly whether any silo has gone dark for a month.

test.method: Track founder hours per silo and tasks bought from freelancers for 1 quarter.
test.measure: Whether any silo goes dark for a month
test.read_point: Monthly, until revenue nears the next stage trigger

title: Write the next hire trigger as a number, not a feeling
hypothesis: If we write the next hire's trigger in the store's own numbers, such as orders per week or days the PO tracker sits stale, then the team stops hiring on a vague feeling of being stretched, because the trigger names the exact point the current owner can no longer keep the artefact current.

signal.check: A hire request cites no number: the PO tracker is a week stale, tickets sit over 48 hours, or reorders are being missed.

expected_effect.size: unknown; sources give stage ranges (about $5M to $10M for a tracker owner, about $30M to $50M for an ERP) but no precision figure

risk.note: A planning exercise; wrong trigger numbers can be revised before any hire is made.

prerequisites: order volume, ticket volume and revenue by month
steps: Pull order volume, ticket volume and revenue by month for the last 12 months.
For a wide catalogue, note that the PO tracker limit hits at a lower revenue than for a hero SKU store.
Write the trigger at or below the point the current owner cannot keep the artefact current.
Check monthly whether the brand's data has crossed the written trigger.

test.method: Compare the written trigger against actual monthly data.
test.measure: orders per week, tickets per week, revenue per month vs the trigger
test.read_point: Monthly review until the trigger is crossed

title: Check whether the ops, media or CS lead is underused before hiring a second person into that seat
hypothesis: If we check whether the current ops manager, media buyer or CS lead is underused before adding a second head into that seat, then the growth target gets met by getting more from the person already there, because a hire added to an underused seat produces someone overworked and underutilized at once.
does_not_apply_when: a capability gap check already showed the current owner near full capacity

signal.check: A growth target arrives with no extra budget, or a hire request is justified only by 'we are stretched'.

expected_effect.size: source claims up to about 2x between the least and most used team member, self-reported

risk.note: A conversation and a check, not a structural change.

steps: Before approving a hire, run the capability gap check with the current seat holder.
Ask if the media buyer spends real time on reporting a tool could produce.
Ask if the CS lead answers tickets a macro could clear.
If key people estimate the manager gets 50% or less of their capability, fix leadership habits first.
Only open the hire once the seat is genuinely full.

test.method: Run the capability gap check with each key person before opening a requisition.
test.measure: self-estimated percent of capability used
test.read_point: Before any hire request is approved

title: Write a hire as the missing store function, never as a generic strong hire
hypothesis: If we name a hire as a demand planner, media buyer, merchandiser or CS lead instead of an A player for management, then the search and the scorecard target real store gaps, because a level or personality title gives the interviewer nothing to check the candidate against.

signal.check: A hire request names a seniority level or a personality trait, not a silo or a function.

expected_effect.size: unknown; 2 sources agree on the approach, no measured lift given

risk.note: A rewrite of the job description, no commitment made yet.

steps: Rewrite the hire request naming 1 store function it fills.
Name 1 artefact from the SOP list it will own.
Name 1 metric the seat should move.
Drop any wording about being 'an A player' or 'a strong manager' with no function attached.

test.method: Review the scorecard before opening the search.
test.measure: presence of 1 named function, 1 artefact and 1 metric on the scorecard
test.read_point: Before the job ad is written

title: At a plateau, hire the archetype the founder is not
hypothesis: If we ask which core function the founder confidently owns, sourcing and product or media and acquisition, and hire against the side they hedge on, then flat revenue starts moving again, because the untended side is usually the real constraint, not a general management gap.
does_not_apply_when: the founder gives a confident, evidenced answer on both sides

signal.check: Revenue is flat for 2 or more quarters and the founder plans to 'do more marketing' or 'fix sourcing' with no evidence of which side is actually strong.

expected_effect.size: unknown; 1 advisor's pattern from 1 self-reported case

risk.note: Founder may be modest about a skill they actually have; confirm the hedge with evidence, not the answer alone.

steps: Ask the founder which core function they own: product and sourcing, or media and acquisition.
Look for a confident, evidenced answer on 1 side, such as supplier terms or sample rounds.
Note hedging, 'I don't know' or 'not sure', on the other side, such as CAC or creative testing.
Confirm the hedge with real evidence before deciding, since a founder can be modest about a real strength.
Write the next hire against the confirmed gap.

test.method: Compare the founder's self-report against actual evidence (supplier terms secured vs CAC trend) before committing to the hire.
test.measure: revenue growth rate over the following 2 quarters

title: Put a planning and ops owner in place before the first demand surge
hypothesis: If we name an ops or planning owner before a viral hit or a peak season arrives, then we avoid selling out on a spike, because nobody was watching the forecast sheet is the direct cause named in the source's own retrospective.
does_not_apply_when: a peak is more than 1 lead time away and an owner is already named

signal.check: The forecast sheet has no owner and a known peak or seasonal window is inside 1 supplier lead time.

expected_effect.size: source's own retrospective estimate: 30 to 40 percent more growth with the role in place, unverified single case

risk.note: A missed peak cannot be replayed; the cost of not naming an owner shows up as lost sales, not a reversible mistake.

steps: Confirm the next peak or launch date and the supplier lead time.
Check if the forecast sheet already has a named owner.
If not, name an ops manager as the owner; a dedicated demand planner is not required until the business can pay for one.
Give the owner the forecast and reorder review procedure to run before the peak.

test.method: Compare sell-through and stockout days for the peak with an owner in place against the last unowned peak.
test.measure: stockout_days and revenue during the peak window
test.read_point: End of the peak or seasonal window

title: When a COO exists, give them product, supply chain, fulfilment and customer service
hypothesis: If the store creates a COO role, then giving it product, supply chain, fulfilment and customer service in one hand cuts handoff gaps, because those 4 areas already read the same PO, tracker and ticket data day to day.
does_not_apply_when: the store has not decided to create a COO seat yet

signal.check: A COO title exists or is being created but its scope is not written down.

expected_effect.size: unknown; source names the 4 areas, gives no timing rule or measured result

risk.note: A scope document; reversible if the split does not work.

steps: Write the COO's 4 areas: tech packs and product, PO and freight, 3PL and delivered on time, tickets and cost per ticket.
Confirm no other role also claims ownership of these artefacts.
Publish the scope where the team can see it.

test.method: Not a split test; a scope-definition check.
test.measure: whether artefact ownership overlaps after the scope is published
test.read_point: 1 month after the scope is published

title: Regroup direct reports when the trading meeting stops surfacing real numbers
hypothesis: If we regroup direct reports under an ops lead and a growth lead once the weekly trading meeting stops allowing fluid discussion, then reorders and 3PL escalations get decided faster, because too many people reporting to the top crowds out real debate.
does_not_apply_when: the weekly meeting still surfaces and resolves real numbers

signal.check: Staff meetings feel crowded and stop producing substantive discussion, with too many people reporting to 1 leader.

expected_effect.size: unknown; the fable's staffing numbers are illustration only, not a store threshold

risk.note: Tell each affected person individually with the reasoning before publishing the change; watch for 'am I being demoted' reactions.

steps: Watch for staff meetings that no longer allow substantive discussion.
List decisions that stall on unclear ownership or too many attendees.
Regroup functions under 1 ops lead and 1 growth lead.
Tell each affected person individually with the reasoning before publishing.
Judge the change by whether reorders and escalations get decided faster.

test.method: Track time from an escalation raised to a decision made, before and after the regroup.
test.measure: days from escalation to decision

title: Give a launch to 1 owner; use a full team only for a multi-SKU seasonal drop
hypothesis: If a single launch brief or creative concept goes to 1 owner, and a team is used only for a multi-SKU drop needing merchandising, creative and ops together, then work that only needs 1 expert stops slowing down in committee, because separable work does not need shared accountability.

signal.check: A single-SKU launch brief is being routed through a committee, or a multi-SKU drop is being handled by 1 person alone.

expected_effect.size: unknown; 2 sources agree on the line between group and team work, no lift measured

risk.note: A staffing decision, reversible for the next launch.

steps: For each upcoming launch, ask whether the work is separable (1 listing, 1 shoot) or interdependent (a drop where a late sample delays the shoot, the PDP and the ads).
Assign separable work to 1 owner.
Assign interdependent, multi-SKU work to a small cross-functional team.
Avoid committees on work 1 expert can do alone.

test.method: Compare time from brief to launch for team-run vs single-owner launches.
test.measure: days from brief to launch
test.read_point: After the next 2 to 3 launches of each type

title: Keep the store's leadership team at 5 to 12 people
hypothesis: If the leadership team, merchandising, growth, retention, ops and finance, stays at 5 to 12 people, then the weekly trading meeting keeps real task division and coverage, because oversized teams suffer poor task division and friction while too-lean teams lack coverage.

signal.check: The trading meeting has grown past 12 attendees, or has fewer than 5 with clear coverage gaps.

expected_effect.size: unknown; 2 sources agree on the range, both conventions with no data

risk.note: A meeting invite list change.

steps: Count who attends the weekly trading meeting.
If more than 12, cut to function owners only, 1 per function even for a large catalogue with several merchandisers.
If fewer than 5, check for a coverage gap in a key function.
Re-check attendance each quarter as the team grows.

test.method: Not a split test; a headcount and coverage check.
test.measure: trading meeting attendee count and function coverage

title: Name a backup for every key artefact, login and supplier relationship
hypothesis: If we name a backup, even the founder, for every ad account login, factory contact and forecast reader, then a single person leaving or being unavailable stops being a business-stopping event, because the store no longer depends on 1 hero holding sole access.

signal.check: 1 person is the only ad account login, the only factory contact, or the only one who can read the forecast.

expected_effect.size: unknown; source calls over-reliance on 1 dominant person 'almost always a big mistake', no percent given

risk.note: Adding a backup does not remove the primary owner's responsibility.

steps: List every artefact from the SOP index, the ad account and the 3PL portal.
For each, check if a named backup exists beyond the primary owner.
Where none exists, add the founder or another team member as backup without reducing the primary owner's accountability.
Review the backup list each quarter or after any role change.

test.method: Audit access and knowledge coverage per artefact.
test.measure: count of artefacts with a named backup

title: Write every role down, then stretch it 1 level up
hypothesis: If we write down which silo, artefacts and metric each role owns and then stretch it 1 level above current comfort, then ownership confusion (2 people thinking they own the promo calendar, or nobody owning returns) goes away, because the stretch sits on top of a defined role instead of replacing it.

signal.check: 2 people believe they own the same task, such as the promo calendar, or nobody claims a task, such as returns.

expected_effect.size: unknown; 4 sources agree on writing roles down, no measured lift

risk.note: A documentation exercise, reversible on the next review.

steps: For each role, write which silo, which artefacts and which metric it owns.
Identify 1 stretch responsibility 1 level above the role's current comfort.
Confirm the stretch is added on top of the role, not a replacement for it.
Publish the written roles where the team can see them.

test.method: Track role-ownership disputes before and after roles are written down.
test.measure: count of role ambiguity incidents per quarter

title: Set scope, cost and review owner before adding any agency pod or contractor roster
hypothesis: If we write scope, cost and a reviewing owner for every vendor before adding an agency pod or contractor roster, then vendor spend gets checked against output, because no source gives a rule for agency vs in-house and the gap has to be closed with a written record instead of assumption.
does_not_apply_when: revenue is below about $1M and the task is a 1-off freelance deliverable

signal.check: A vendor, agency or contractor roster has no written scope, cost or named reviewer.

expected_effect.size: unknown; no source gives a rule for agency vs in-house structure

risk.note: A documentation step before or alongside an existing vendor relationship.

prerequisites: current vendor list, scope, cost and reviewer
steps: List every current agency, pod or contractor with their scope and cost.
Name 1 person who reviews their output.
For a scarce skill, such as a senior media buyer, decide whether to learn it internally or bring in a paid specialist.
Write this into the brand record before adding a new vendor.

test.method: Not a split test; a governance checklist.
test.measure: share of vendors with written scope, cost and a named reviewer

title: Set a cadence and async rules for a founder-plus-contractors roster or agency pod
hypothesis: If we publish the 1 current priority number, send a written recap after every contractor call, and run accountability through the founder with published deadlines, then a contractor roster stays aligned without shared context, because contractors lack the ambient information an in-house team picks up on its own.

signal.check: Contractors or an agency pod get no written recap after calls, and priorities live only in the founder's head.

expected_effect.size: unknown; adapted from a team-health framework, no store measurement given

risk.note: A communication habit, easy to adjust.

steps: Publish the current priority number where every contractor can see it.
Send a short written recap after every contractor call stating what was decided and by when.
Set the 1 overarching goal per client or contractor engagement.
Run accountability through the founder with published deadlines and progress reviews, not peer pressure.
For an agency pod, run cascading messaging at the end of every client call.

test.method: Track missed handoffs or repeated misunderstandings with contractors before and after the cadence starts.
test.measure: count of contractor misalignment incidents per month

title: Give marketplace channels their own named owner, separate from the DTC silos
hypothesis: If a marketplace channel, such as Amazon, Walmart or Meta Shop, gets 1 named owner separate from the 5 DTC silos, then its listing, ad account and stock stop hiding inside an existing silo, because the channel's mechanics differ enough from DTC to need its own accountable person.
does_not_apply_when: the store runs no marketplace channel

signal.check: The marketplace listing, its ad account, or its stock has no single named owner.

expected_effect.size: unknown; no library source, verify against brand data before use

risk.note: A naming exercise; reversible if roles change.

steps: Confirm the store runs at least 1 marketplace channel.
Name 1 owner for the listing, the marketplace ad account and marketplace stock.
Add marketplace stock as its own row in the forecast sheet.
Check monthly that the owner name has not gone stale.

test.method: Not a lab test; an ownership and data-accuracy check.
test.measure: marketplace stock accuracy and listing update frequency

title: Name a subscription retention owner as its own silo
hypothesis: If a store running a subscription programme names 1 owner for win-back, dunning and churn, then churn and failed payments stop sitting in nobody's weekly review, because folding subscription work into CS or marketing hides the metric that matters most for that book of business.
does_not_apply_when: the store runs no subscription programme

signal.check: Monthly churn and failed-payment recovery do not appear in any weekly review.

expected_effect.size: unknown; no library source, verify against brand data before use

risk.note: A naming exercise for an existing programme.

steps: Confirm the store runs a subscription programme.
Name 1 owner for win-back, dunning and churn.
Put monthly churn and failed-payment recovery on the scoreboard.
Review the numbers with the owner in the weekly meeting.

test.method: Not a lab test; an ownership and reporting check.
test.measure: subscription_churn and failed-payment recovery rate

title: Run an org chart vs revenue-stage review every quarter
hypothesis: If we run a quarterly review that lists every silo, every artefact owner and the store's stage against known revenue triggers, then the next hire trigger gets caught early, because the review flags a stale artefact or an owner covering too many at once as a capacity risk before it causes a miss.

signal.check: No review has been run in the last quarter listing silo owners, artefact owners and their cadence.

expected_effect.size: unknown; procedure built from single-source stage triggers, no measured result given

risk.note: A read-only review; no operational change until a hire or reassignment follows.

prerequisites: revenue and order volume by month
steps: List the 5 silos and write the owner of each.
List the operating artefacts and their owner and update cadence.
Mark revenue stage against the sourced triggers: under about $1M founder holds all ops roles, about $5M to $10M a dedicated tracker owner, about $30M to $50M consider an ERP.
Flag any artefact with a stale update or an owner who also owns 3 or more other artefacts as a capacity risk.
Run the capability gap check before proposing any hire.
Output the org plan by stage.

test.method: Run the review each quarter and compare capacity-risk flags over time.
test.measure: count of capacity-risk flags and artefacts with no owner

title: Decide the next hire with a written trigger, a defined role and comp options for the founder to choose
hypothesis: If every hire decision comes with a written trigger in the store's own numbers, a role tied to the missing function, and at least 2 comp options within margin, then the founder makes a faster, better-informed hire call, because the decision is reduced to approving prepared evidence instead of debating from scratch.

signal.check: A hire is being discussed with no written trigger, no named function, and no comp option list.

expected_effect.size: unknown; procedure combines several single-source rules, no measured lift given

risk.note: A planning document; the human still decides whether to hire.

steps: Ask the founder which core function they own, and note any hedging.
If the store has plateaued, run the bottleneck diagnosis first; let the constraint decide the role.
Define the role around the missing function; write what good looks like as behaviours and results.
Write the trigger in the store's own numbers, at or below the point the current owner cannot keep the artefact current.
List at least 2 comp options for the founder: cash within margin, performance pay, or equity if margin is thin.
Consider an assignment change or a contractor before a new head.
Hand the completed hiring plan to the founder; the founder decides.

test.method: Track how many prepared hiring plans the founder approves without further back-and-forth.
test.measure: share of hiring plans approved on first review
test.read_point: After each hiring plan is submitted

title: Score a store hire on whether they will flag a bad brief out loud, not only on channel skill
hypothesis: If the hiring scorecard scores vulnerability, conflict on ideas, commitment, peer accountability and results over ego alongside channel or platform skill, then bad launches and weak briefs get flagged before they ship, because a candidate who only knows the tools but stays quiet in a room will not stop a mistake.

signal.check: The hiring scorecard lists only tools and platform experience, with no behaviour row.

expected_effect.size: unknown; 2 sources agree on the behaviours, no measured lift given

risk.note: A scorecard edit, reversible before the next search.

steps: Add 1 line per behaviour to the scorecard: vulnerability-based trust, conflict on ideas, commitment to group decisions, holding peers accountable, results over ego.
Add drive toward a defined next level and understanding of the company's objectives and ethics for a marketing hire.
Write 1 store situation to probe each behaviour, such as a launch that slipped or a test that lost.
Use the scorecard in every interview for the role.

test.method: Track whether new hires flag a weak brief or plan in their first quarter.
test.measure: count of bad briefs or plans flagged by the new hire in the first 90 days

title: Name 1 search owner, screen fast, then run 1 deep round with the whole team
hypothesis: If 1 person owns the search and runs short first screens, then no offer goes out without a deep finalist round involving the whole team, then hiring moves fast without skipping the team input that predicts fit, because speed and team judgment do not have to trade off against each other.

signal.check: The search has no single named owner, or an offer is being considered without the team meeting the finalist.

expected_effect.size: unknown; both sources give single-case timing examples (3-minute screens for 8, 3 hours with the finalist), not a rule

risk.note: A process change; can be adjusted for the next search.

steps: Name 1 person to own the search end to end.
Run short first screens across the shortlist to cut quickly.
Run a deep finalist round, several hours, with the whole team.
Base the deep round on a live artefact, such as the forecast sheet, a losing ad set, or last week's ticket queue.
Do not send an offer without the deep round and team input.

test.method: Track days from search opening to offer, and post-hire fit at 90 days.
test.measure: hiring cycle time and 90-day fit rating
test.read_point: Offer stage and 90 days after start

title: Debate internal promotion vs external hire openly, then have the leader decide and state the criterion
hypothesis: If we debate an internal promotion vs an external hire openly, invite last input, and have the leader decide and state the criterion, such as whether the candidate can grow the function, then the team accepts the outcome faster, because the reasoning was heard, not hidden.

signal.check: A seat opens above someone already on the team, such as a senior CS agent when the CS lead leaves, and the decision is being made quietly.

expected_effect.size: unknown; 1 source, 1 fable case

risk.note: A decision process, not a structural change.

steps: State the open seat and the internal candidate under consideration.
Debate openly whether the internal candidate can grow into the function.
Invite last input from the team before deciding.
Have the leader decide and state the criterion used, out loud.

test.method: Not a split test; a decision process check.
test.measure: whether the decision and its criterion were communicated to the team

title: Interview candidates with the sourced question set, not an invented rubric
hypothesis: If interviewers ask only the sourced questions, the next-challenge question, the native genius probe asked 3 ways, and which core function they own, then the interview surfaces real signal instead of an invented rubric presented as validated, because these questions come from the sources and everything else must be marked as the human's own design.

signal.check: An interview guide includes a scoring rubric or trial task with no source, presented as if it were tested.

expected_effect.size: unknown; each question is from a single source or advisor pattern

risk.note: A question-list edit.

steps: Ask: 'What is the next challenge for you?' and 'What is getting in the way of your being successful?'
Ask the native genius probe 3 ways: what you do better than anything else, without effort, without being asked, without needing to be paid.
Ask: 'How have you broken through a previous goal?'
For an ops, media or merchandising candidate, ask which core function they own and watch for hedging.
Mark any trial task or rubric not listed here as 'not sourced: human designs'.

test.method: Compare interview notes against 90-day performance for hires screened with the sourced questions.
test.measure: correlation between interview signal and 90-day performance

title: Write the job ad honest and demanding about the real workload
hypothesis: If the job ad states the real order volume, the real ticket load and the artefact the hire will own, instead of generic enthusiasm language, then well-suited applicants apply even though the work sounds hard, because an honest, demanding ad filters for people who want that exact challenge.

signal.check: The job ad reads as generic ('fast-paced, dynamic team') with no real numbers or named artefact.

expected_effect.size: unknown; 1 anecdote (Shackleton's ad) is the only evidence

risk.note: A copy change to the job ad.

steps: State the real order volume and ticket load in the ad.
Name the artefact the hire will own.
State the hard parts honestly instead of hiding them.
Remove generic buzzwords that say nothing about the actual job.

test.method: Compare applicant fit rate and quit rate in the first 90 days between the old and new ad copy.
test.measure: applicant fit rate and early quit rate
test.read_point: After the next search closes and 90 days after the hire starts

title: Look for talent past the org chart before opening an external search
hypothesis: If we look at the freelance designer, the warehouse packer who spots defects, or the support rep with an unusual strength before opening an external search, then a real gap gets filled from inside the store's own network, because an unusual strength already proven on the job predicts more than an unseen candidate's resume.

signal.check: A new external search is opening without first checking whether an existing contractor, packer or support rep already shows the needed strength.

expected_effect.size: unknown; 1 anecdote describes a large but atypical outcome, not a typical rate

risk.note: A scouting step before external hiring; no commitment yet.

steps: Before posting an external search, list contractors, packers and support staff who touch the relevant work.
Ask managers to name any unusual strength observed in someone outside the target role.
Example: the CS agent who answers sizing questions best could own the PDP fit guide and returns-reason review.
Trial the person on a piece of the role before committing to a full move.

test.method: Trial the identified person on a defined slice of the role for a set period.
test.measure: output quality on the trial slice vs the role's target metric

title: Use equity or performance pay for a scarce role only when margin cannot support market cash
hypothesis: If we check margin first and use equity or performance pay only when cash cannot support market pay for a scarce seat, such as a senior media buyer, then the store keeps the hire without over-committing cash, because equity is given up, not free, and should be a fallback, not a first move.
does_not_apply_when: margin already supports market cash pay for the role

signal.check: A scarce hire, such as a senior media buyer, cannot be paid market cash from current margin.

expected_effect.size: 1 unverified case cites 'multiple hundreds of thousands of dollars a year' for a top media buyer

risk.note: Equity given up is not free and cannot be easily reversed; check current market pay for the role before committing.

steps: Check contribution margin before proposing any comp lever.
If margin supports market cash, pay market cash.
If not, offer performance pay or equity as an addition, not a replacement for base pay.
State clearly to the candidate and the founder that equity is given up, not free.
Check current market pay for senior ecommerce roles before finalising the offer.

test.method: Track fill rate and retention for scarce roles hired with a comp lever vs cash-only offers.
test.measure: offer acceptance rate and 12-month retention
test.read_point: At offer stage and 12 months after start

title: Walk every new hire through the live operating artefacts in week 1, not just team norms
hypothesis: If each existing team member teaches the newcomer 1 part of the operating model, the PO tracker, the forecast, the CS routing rules, then by the end of week 1 the newcomer can name every artefact owner, because seeing the real process in use beats a generic culture orientation.

signal.check: Onboarding covers only team culture and norms, with no walkthrough of the actual operating artefacts.

expected_effect.size: unknown; 2 sources agree on the approach, no measured lift given

risk.note: An onboarding checklist addition.

prerequisites: team has a written goal and roles
steps: Assign each existing member 1 part of the operating model to teach the newcomer.
Walk through every peer's role and the current overarching goal and scoreboard.
Compare the newcomer's working style with the team's and describe how peers tend to disagree.
Put the newcomer into a live debate the same day.
Let them watch peers hold each other accountable.
Expect a short storming period and do not read it as failure.

test.method: Quiz the newcomer at the end of week 1 on artefact owners and the overarching goal.
test.measure: share of artefact owners the newcomer can name correctly

title: Try an assignment change before adding headcount for an underperforming owner
hypothesis: If we try moving an underperforming owner to a different function for 1 quarter before hiring a replacement, then the store may find the right seat for that person without the cost of a new hire, because a poor fit in 1 role does not always mean the person lacks value elsewhere.

signal.check: A replacement hire is being discussed for an owner who is underperforming in their current seat.

expected_effect.size: unknown; 1 fable case only

risk.note: A 1-quarter trial; reverse if the new seat does not work either.

steps: Name the underperforming owner and the seat under discussion.
Identify a different function where their behaviour suggests a better fit, such as an ops manager who keeps redesigning the collection page becoming the merchandiser.
Try the swap for 1 quarter.
Judge the swap on that silo's own metric before deciding on a hire.

test.method: Measure the target metric for the new seat over 1 quarter.
test.measure: the reassigned silo's own metric (for example, sell-through for merchandising)

title: Confront a channel or merchandiser hoarding results before removing them, with a real choice to change
hypothesis: If a media buyer or merchandiser who hits targets while withholding test data or starving other channels gets a private conversation naming the specific behaviour and a real choice to change, then the store either fixes the behaviour or removes the person cleanly, because waiting too long to act is the common, costly error.

signal.check: 1 channel's number looks great while the blended number or the test log goes quiet.

expected_effect.size: unknown; 2 sources agree tolerance, not the person, is usually the real failure

risk.note: A departure cannot be undone; the human makes the final call, not the agent.

steps: Name the specific behaviour, such as the test log not being updated.
Hold a private conversation citing the specifics, not general complaints.
Offer a real, complete and fast choice to change.
Expect denial or blame; repeat the specifics calmly.
If departure follows, put severance and terms in writing with HR.
Attribute the cost to the delay in acting, not only to the person.

test.method: Track the blended metric and test log activity for 1 quarter after the conversation.
test.measure: roas_blended and test log update frequency

title: Set comp bands for media buyer, CS lead and ops manager before opening a search
hypothesis: If comp bands for the common ecom roles are set against contribution margin before a search opens, then a candidate's pay question does not stall the process, because the band already exists instead of being negotiated live for the first time.

signal.check: A search is open with no written comp band, and pay gets decided only when a candidate asks.

expected_effect.size: unknown; only 1 unverified figure exists for media buyer pay, no band for CS lead or ops manager in any source

risk.note: A pay band, adjustable before the next search.

steps: Check current market pay for the role before setting the band.
Set the band against contribution margin, not revenue.
Write the band into the role scorecard before the ad goes out.
Revisit the band each time the role reopens.

test.method: Not a split test; a pre-search readiness check.
test.measure: presence of a written comp band before the ad posts

title: Use a structured job description template naming silo, artefacts and metric for every role
hypothesis: If every store role uses a template naming its silo, the artefacts it owns, the metric it moves and the trigger that opened it, then job ads stop reading as free text with no way to check candidates against the role, because the template forces the same clarity every time.

signal.check: Job descriptions are written free-text with no consistent structure across roles.

expected_effect.size: unknown; no source gives a template, this is a store-designed fix for a named gap

risk.note: A template, easy to revise.

steps: Build a template with 4 fields: silo, artefacts owned, metric moved, trigger number that opened the role.
Fill the template for every open or newly created role.
Use the filled template as the base for the job ad and the role scorecard.
Store completed templates for reuse on the next hire in the same role.

test.method: Not a split test; a documentation coverage check.
test.measure: share of open roles with a filled template

title: Run performance reviews tied to each seat's own metric, separate from pay and team-health scores
hypothesis: If each seat gets a review tied to its own metric, delivered-on-time for ops, cost per ticket for CS, blended CAC for growth, sell-through for merchandising, and this stays separate from the team-health assessment and from pay decisions, then reviews give real signal instead of mixing morale scores with performance scores.

signal.check: Performance reviews use only a generic template with no seat-specific metric, or are combined with the team-health assessment.

expected_effect.size: unknown; no source gives a cadence or template, this is a store-designed fix

risk.note: A review process change.

steps: For each seat, name the 1 metric it should be reviewed against.
Set a review cadence for each seat.
Keep the review separate from the team-health assessment (P5) and out of pay decisions.
Record each review with target and actual against the metric.

test.method: Not a split test; a process separation check.
test.measure: share of reviews tied to a named seat metric, kept separate from pay

title: Run a hire end to end: name a search owner, write an honest ad, screen fast, then deep round with the team
hypothesis: If a hire runs through 1 named search owner, an honest and demanding ad, fast first screens, a deep finalist round with the whole team, and only the sourced interview questions, then the candidate who reaches an offer has been checked on both skill and store-fit behaviours, because each step closes a specific gap the sources warn about.

signal.check: A hire is in progress with no single search owner, a generic ad, or no planned deep round with the team.

expected_effect.size: unknown; the procedure combines several single-source steps, no combined measured result given

risk.note: No offer goes out without the deep round; rollback is simply not extending an offer.

steps: Name 1 search owner.
Write an honest, demanding ad that states the hard parts.
Run short first screens across the shortlist.
Run a deep finalist round with the whole team, several hours, on a live artefact.
Ask only sourced questions: next challenge, what gets in the way, the native genius probe, which core function they own.
Score against the behaviour bar: trust, conflict on ideas, commit, hold peers accountable, results over ego, drive.
If internal vs external is open, run the open debate and have the leader decide and state the criterion.
Recommend to the founder; the founder decides.

test.method: Track every interviewer's use of the same questions and whether the team's input is recorded before the decision.
test.measure: process compliance and 90-day fit rating of the hire
test.read_point: At offer stage and 90 days after start

title: Fix the lowest broken trust or conflict layer before treating a missed launch as a results problem
hypothesis: If we treat a missed launch or a silent stockout as a signal to check trust and conflict first, not results alone, then the real cause surfaces faster, because the dysfunction chain runs from absent trust to fear of conflict to lack of commitment to avoided accountability to poor results, in that order.

signal.check: Drops slip and reorders miss while meetings stay calm with no visible conflict.

expected_effect.size: unknown; 1 source, a framework not a measured result

risk.note: A diagnostic lens, not a structural change.

steps: When a launch slips or a stockout happens quietly, run the team assessment (P5) instead of only reviewing the results.
Read the scores to find the lowest broken layer: trust, conflict, commitment, accountability, or results.
Start remediation at that layer, not at whichever layer shows the visible pain.

test.method: Run the assessment after the next slipped launch and compare the lowest layer to the visible symptom.
test.measure: which dysfunction layer scores lowest vs where the pain first showed
test.read_point: After the next missed launch or stockout

title: Have the leader admit a mistake first, out loud, before asking others to show weakness
hypothesis: If the founder or lead names their own missed forecast or mistake first and visibly, then the merchandiser and media buyer start admitting over-orders and losing tests sooner, because trust is built through the leader committing first, not through a policy statement.

signal.check: Bad numbers reach the founder late, or team members hide mistakes until they are found out.

expected_effect.size: unknown; 3 sources agree on the mechanism, no measured lift given

risk.note: A leadership behaviour, not a structural change.

steps: Before the next team meeting, identify 1 real mistake or missed number of your own.
Name it plainly in the meeting, without minimising it.
Ask for help on it rather than presenting it as already solved.
Watch whether team members start naming their own misses sooner over the following weeks.

test.method: Track how long it takes for a bad number (an over-order, a losing test) to reach the founder, before and after.
test.measure: days from a bad result occurring to it being reported

title: Pair the team dysfunction assessment score with 1 real store metric each quarter
hypothesis: If the 15-statement dysfunction assessment is paired with 1 store metric each quarter, such as repeat rate, ticket backlog or launch on-time percent, then the team-health score stops floating free of business results, because a low trust score with a rising ticket backlog says more than either number alone.

signal.check: The team assessment is run with no linked store metric, or the metric is only revenue.

expected_effect.size: unknown; pass 1 addition, not a source-stated measurement

risk.note: A reporting addition.

prerequisites: team assessment run at least once
steps: Run the 15-statement assessment (P5) each quarter.
Pick 1 store metric that most matches the visible pain, such as repeat rate, ticket backlog or launch on-time percent.
Report the assessment bands and the chosen metric side by side.
Compare the spread between members, not only the average.

test.method: Track the dysfunction score and the paired metric together each quarter.
test.measure: the chosen store metric alongside the dysfunction band

title: Treat conflict as about the offer or reorder, not the person, and expect it to look heated
hypothesis: If the team frames disagreement as being about the discount depth, the creative, or the reorder quantity, and not about the person, then the promo calendar stops changing by side message after a meeting that agreed on everything, because healthy conflict can look heated and still be constructive.

signal.check: The meeting agrees on everything and the promo calendar still changes by side message afterward.

expected_effect.size: unknown; 2 sources agree, no measured lift given

risk.note: A meeting norm, adjustable.

steps: State the norm at the start of the meeting: disagree about the idea, not the person.
Watch for signs of destructive conflict: energy diverted, sub-groups forming, name-calling.
Encourage constructive conflict: issues opened and clarified, more people involved, emotion released.
Note any decision that changes by side message after the meeting as a signal the real disagreement was never raised.

test.method: Track how many decisions get reversed or changed outside the meeting within 1 week.
test.measure: count of post-meeting reversals per month

title: Treat a recurring, evenly split agenda item as a fear-of-conflict signal and decide it by the next meeting
hypothesis: If a recurring agenda item with a roughly even split, such as discount depth or a 3PL switch, gets routed to a forced decision by the next meeting instead of being taken off-line, then the issue stops resurfacing meeting after meeting, because avoiding conflict does not save time and suppressed disagreement goes underground.

signal.check: The same decision appears on 3 or more agendas with a roughly even split and no resolution.

expected_effect.size: unknown; 1 source

risk.note: A meeting discipline, adjustable.

steps: Track how many meetings an unresolved item has appeared on.
At 3 appearances, flag it as a fear-of-conflict signal rather than a genuinely undecidable issue.
Set a deadline: the item must be decided by the next meeting.
Route it through the decision-framing process (R82) if it is high stakes.

test.method: Count how many agenda items exceed 3 appearances before and after the rule.
test.measure: count of items appearing on 3+ agendas without a decision

title: Assign 1 person in every meeting to surface buried disagreement
hypothesis: If 1 person is assigned to ask, out loud, whether the ops or CS owner can really cover the promo volume, and the leader does not step in to protect people from that discomfort, then buried disagreement surfaces during the meeting instead of after it, because someone's explicit job is to mine for the conflict others avoid.

signal.check: The ops or CS owner never pushes back on growth's plan in the meeting, though they raise concerns privately afterward.

expected_effect.size: unknown; 1 source

risk.note: A meeting role assignment.

steps: Name 1 person per meeting as the conflict miner.
Have them directly ask the quiet function owner for their honest view.
When people retreat from the discomfort, interrupt to say it is expected.
Confirm afterward that raising it was useful.
The leader does not break up the conflict early to protect people.

test.method: Track how often a previously silent function owner raises a concern in the meeting itself.
test.measure: count of in-meeting pushback instances per month

title: Decide on clarity and buy-in, not full agreement, when a price, promo or PO stalls
hypothesis: If the leader decides once everyone has been heard, rather than waiting for full agreement on a price, promo or PO, then ordinary decisions stop stalling, because people mainly need to be heard, not to get their way, and proceeding on what is agreed while resolving the rest as work continues counts as real commitment.

signal.check: A decision is delayed waiting for everyone to fully agree, though everyone has already been heard.

expected_effect.size: unknown; 2 sources agree once the term 'consensus' is defined the same way

risk.note: A decision norm, adjustable.

steps: Hear every relevant person's view on the decision.
Proceed on whatever is already agreed, such as the launch date.
Have the leader decide the remaining open point, such as the discount depth.
Do not wait for 100 percent agreement before moving.

test.method: Track time from a decision being raised to it being made.
test.measure: decision cycle time in days

title: Decide ordinary calls boldly instead of waiting for more data
hypothesis: If ordinary decisions, a subject line, a collection sort order, a small reorder, get decided quickly and changed just as quickly if wrong, then the team stops freezing on low-stakes calls, because delaying for more data on an everyday decision breeds paralysis without adding real value.

signal.check: A low-stakes decision, such as a banner colour or a subject line, has been open for weeks.

expected_effect.size: unknown; 1 source for the wording

risk.note: Applies only to reversible, low-stakes calls; use R81's split to route high-stakes calls elsewhere.

steps: Classify the decision as everyday, not high stakes, using the debate-worthiness check.
Decide with the information already on hand.
If the decision turns out wrong, change it without ceremony.
Avoid opening a debate process for decisions this small.

test.method: Track how many everyday decisions sit open longer than 1 week.
test.measure: count of everyday decisions open past 1 week

title: Reduce fear of deciding with deadlines, a stated worst case, and small pilots
hypothesis: If every decision gets a deadline, a stated worst case up front, and low-stakes items get real but lighter discussion, then a team that has spent weeks on a banner colour while freezing the peak PO starts moving again, because naming the worst case shows it is survivable and recalibrates an over-studying team.

signal.check: Weeks pass on a low-stakes decision while a genuinely important one, such as the peak PO, sits frozen.

expected_effect.size: unknown; 2 sources agree on the mechanism

risk.note: A decision-making habit.

steps: Set and honour a deadline for every open decision, not only deliverable dates.
State the worst case out loud before deciding, such as the reorder selling through late or the promo margin dropping.
For low-stakes items, allow real discussion but less analysis.
Before committing on a bigger item, run a small pilot on 1 SKU or 1 geo where possible.
Name the irreducible risk openly rather than hiding it.

test.method: Track decision cycle time for items with and without a stated deadline and worst case.
test.measure: decision cycle time

title: Run cascading messaging in the last 10 minutes of every staff meeting
hypothesis: If the last 10 minutes of every staff meeting and every agency or contractor call are used to agree what CS, the agency and the 3PL will be told, then managers who sat in the same meeting stop saying different things afterward, because a shared, explicit recap catches disagreement about what was decided while it is still cheap to fix.

signal.check: Different managers describe a recent decision differently to CS, an agency or a 3PL.

expected_effect.size: unknown; 1 source

risk.note: A meeting-ending habit.

steps: Reserve the last 10 minutes of every staff meeting for cascading messaging.
Review the decisions made in the meeting.
Agree exactly what will be told to CS, the agency and the 3PL, and by whom.
Mark what stays confidential, such as a price rise or a supplier change.
Treat any disagreement about what was decided as a cheap early catch.
For contractor or agency calls, send the same recap in writing right after the call.

test.method: Track incidents where 2 people gave different accounts of a decision to an outside party.
test.measure: count of message inconsistency incidents per month

title: Make peer pressure the primary accountability mechanism for full-time staff
hypothesis: If peers are expected and enabled to call out a missed commitment before the leader has to step in, then the team stops staying silent while waiting for the leader to enforce every standard, because a leader who is the only source of discipline creates an accountability vacuum.
does_not_apply_when: the roster is contractors, an agency or a 3PL rather than full-time peers

signal.check: Only the leader ever calls out a missed deadline or a dropped commitment; peers stay silent.

expected_effect.size: unknown; 1 source

risk.note: A team norm; use written SLAs instead for contractors and vendors.

steps: State the expectation that peers, not only the leader, hold each other to commitments.
In the weekly review, ask peers directly whether a driver is on or behind track, before the leader comments.
Model the leader stepping in only as a last resort, not routinely.
For contractors and vendors, use written deadlines and SLAs instead.

test.method: Track how often a peer, not the leader, raises a missed commitment first.
test.measure: count of peer-raised accountability incidents per month

title: Publish every goal, owner and standard where the whole team can see it
hypothesis: If every goal, owner and standard is published visibly, including to contractors, then progress reviews run against a shared, checkable record, because 3 sources agree that a visible scoreboard lets people manage themselves instead of waiting to be asked.

signal.check: Goals, owners or standards exist only in someone's head or in a private document.

expected_effect.size: unknown; 3 sources agree, no measured lift given

risk.note: A documentation and publishing step.

steps: List every current goal, owner and standard.
Publish it somewhere the whole team, including contractors, can see it.
Run simple, regular progress reviews against the published list.
Check each scoreboard line has 1 name and a target.

test.method: Not a split test; a visibility and review-cadence check.
test.measure: share of goals, owners and standards visible to the whole team

title: Build the scoreboard from ecommerce categories, not a generic software-company list
hypothesis: If the store's scoreboard uses 5 to 7 lines built from repeat rate, contribution margin, days of stock, ticket backlog and delivered-on-time, reviewed monthly, instead of a generic category list or revenue alone, then the team tracks what actually predicts store health, because revenue and profit alone lag and give too few chances to correct on a quarterly cycle.
does_not_apply_when: a scoreboard with ecom-specific categories, monthly review and named owners already exists

signal.check: The scoreboard lists revenue alone, or categories copied from a generic business template, reviewed only quarterly.

expected_effect.size: unknown; 2 sources agree on the shape, no measured lift given

risk.note: A reporting change, adjustable each quarter.

prerequisites: revenue and cost data on hand
leadership team available to build it together
steps: In small groups, propose result categories without quantifying them yet.
Merge and cut to 5 to 7 simple, daily-actionable categories: repeat rate, contribution margin, days of stock, ticket backlog, delivered-on-time.
Reject revenue or profit alone as the scoreboard since both lag.
For a subscription store, swap repeat rate for monthly churn; for a marketplace-heavy store, add marketplace share of orders.
Assign 1 named owner per category who states target and result at every review.
Set the review to monthly, not quarterly.
Publish it where everyone, including contractors, can see it.

test.method: Run the scoreboard for 1 quarter and compare decision speed against the prior revenue-only reporting.
test.measure: each scoreboard line's target vs actual, reviewed monthly

title: Make the leadership team, not the department, each leader's first loyalty
hypothesis: If each leader treats the leadership team's shared result as more important than their own department's number, such as the media buyer prioritising the blended number over 1 channel's ROAS, then bad news reaches the founder sooner, because a 'my department first' stance hides problems locally instead of surfacing them.

signal.check: A stockout or a problem in 1 function is told only to the founder, or a leader trades a company commitment for departmental goodwill.

expected_effect.size: unknown; 1 source

risk.note: A leadership norm.

steps: State the norm that the leadership team's shared result comes before any 1 department's number.
Watch for go-betweens or bad news kept local, such as a stockout told only to the founder.
Ask each leader in the weekly review to report on the shared number first, then their own.
Address any pattern of trading company commitments for departmental goodwill directly.

test.method: Track how quickly a functional problem reaches the whole leadership team rather than only the founder.
test.measure: days from a problem occurring to the whole leadership team knowing

title: Confirm the team actually wants to win before running trust or accountability tools on it
hypothesis: If we confirm whether the team cares when the drop misses its sell-through target before running trust, conflict or accountability exercises, then those tools get applied where they can actually work, because no amount of process compensates for a team that exists only to exist.

signal.check: Morale does not move when the team misses a goal.

expected_effect.size: unknown; 1 source

risk.note: A low desire-to-win signal points to a deeper staffing or morale issue that team-health tools alone will not fix.

steps: After the next missed goal, watch whether morale visibly moves.
Ask the team directly whether they care about hitting the number.
If the answer is no or flat, address the underlying staffing or motivation issue before running P5 or P9.
Only run the team-health tools once desire to win is confirmed.

test.method: Observe morale and engagement after the next missed goal before deciding whether to run team-health tools.
test.measure: qualitative read of morale response to a missed goal

title: Weight rewards to collective results and keep 360 feedback out of pay
hypothesis: If rewards lean toward collective outcomes, such as contribution margin or repeat rate, instead of 1 channel's ROAS or 1 SKU's sell-through, and 360 feedback stays out of pay decisions, then individuals stop optimising their own number at the team's expense, because 360 without training becomes disguised criticism rather than useful signal.

signal.check: Bonuses or incentives are tied to 1 channel's or 1 person's individual number rather than a shared result, or 360 feedback influences pay.

expected_effect.size: unknown; 2 sources agree on the direction, no measured lift given

risk.note: Changing comp structure affects morale; the human sets final pay terms.

steps: Review current bonus or incentive structures for any individual-channel or individual-SKU metric.
Shift the weighting toward collective outcomes: contribution margin, repeat rate.
Tie rewards to results, not effort alone.
Remove 360 feedback from any pay-linked process.
Have the human finalise any pay change.

test.method: Track whether test-log sharing and cross-channel cooperation change after the reward shift.
test.measure: other:test_log_activity and contribution_margin trend

title: Run the 15-statement team dysfunction assessment each quarter and act on the lowest band
hypothesis: If every team member scores the 15 statements each quarter and the team discusses the spread and the lowest layer, then the team catches a trust or accountability slip before it shows up as a missed launch, because the assessment surfaces where the chain is broken before results suffer.

signal.check: No team assessment has been run in the last quarter, or after a senior change.

expected_effect.size: unknown; 1 source, unvalidated instrument

risk.note: Results are development data, never linked to pay.

prerequisites: a team of peers willing to answer honestly
steps: Each member scores 15 statements 3 Usually, 2 Sometimes, or 1 Rarely.
Total per dysfunction: trust, conflict, commitment, accountability, results (max 9 each).
Read the bands: 8 to 9 probably fine, 6 to 7 could be a problem, 3 to 5 probably needs addressing, treated as rough only.
Compare the spread between members on each dysfunction.
Discuss as a team and agree 1 behaviour change for the next quarter.
Start remediation at the lowest broken layer.
Re-run each quarter or after any senior change.

test.method: Compute totals in code, not by eye, and track the lowest band over consecutive quarters.
test.measure: dysfunction band scores and spread across members
test.read_point: Quarterly, or after a senior change

title: Set the scoreboard and 1 overarching goal through an open group process, not a leader's private list
hypothesis: If the leadership team proposes categories, argues out every candidate overarching goal until 1 survives, and the leader states the final number and reasoning after hearing everyone, then the team commits to a real target instead of a leader-imposed one, because people accept being overruled when the reasoning is explained.

signal.check: The scoreboard or the overarching goal was set by the leader alone with no group debate.

expected_effect.size: unknown; 1 source, fable-based process

risk.note: Re-run the process at the next quarterly session if the goal proves wrong; avoid adding a second goal.

prerequisites: revenue and cost data on hand
steps: Have small groups propose result categories, not yet quantified.
Merge and cut to 5 to 7 simple, daily-actionable categories.
Assign 1 named owner per category who states target and result at every review.
Set the review to monthly.
List every plausible overarching goal and argue each against the others until 1 remains, rejecting renamed duplicates.
Have the leader set the final number and deadline after hearing everyone and explain the reasoning to whoever was overruled.
Map what each function must do to make the number possible.
Record it where everyone, including contractors, can see it.

test.method: Track whether the team can restate the goal and their own driver correctly 1 month later.
test.measure: share of team members who can correctly restate the goal
test.read_point: 1 month after the goal is set

title: Book the post-peak check-in before the peak starts, expecting a firefighting relapse
hypothesis: If the team books a post-peak review before the peak begins, then the usual reversion to firefighting right after a peak season gets caught and corrected sooner, because guarded regression after any intense period is the typical first response and real change takes months, not 1 offsite.

signal.check: No check-in is scheduled for right after the next peak or seasonal push.

expected_effect.size: unknown; 3 sources agree relapse is typical, no measured lift given

risk.note: A calendar booking, easy to move.

steps: Before the next peak begins, book a check-in for 2 to 4 weeks after it ends.
At the check-in, ask whether the team has reverted to firefighting.
Re-confirm goals, roles and norms if drift has happened.
Treat drift as natural, not a personal failure, since people sit on several teams at once.

test.method: Compare process adherence (meeting cadence kept, artefacts updated) before and after the post-peak check-in.
test.measure: other:artefact_update_adherence

title: Run the commit, check-in, close loop on goals, roles and norms for any team
hypothesis: If a team runs 1 dedicated conversation to commit on goals, roles and norms, checks in on a written cadence, and closes any gap with 1 small specific step, then a late PDP upload with no owner stops recurring, because naming the small fix and changing the surrounding environment closes the gap between what was agreed and what actually happens.

signal.check: The PDP upload, or a similar recurring task, is late again and nobody owns it.

expected_effect.size: unknown; 1 source for the loop, agreement from 2 others on repetition

risk.note: A recurring facilitation habit.

steps: Commit: hold 1 conversation on goals (what), roles (who does what) and norms (how we share information and decide), kept few and simple.
Check in on a written cadence: are we still committed, does our working style still hold, how do we decide now.
Close: name the gap between what was said and what is done, pick 1 small specific change, and alter the surroundings to support it, such as a template or a visible board.
Apply realistic optimism: name what will likely block the fix.
Return to the check-in step on the next cycle.

test.method: Track whether the same recurring task keeps missing its date over 3 cycles.
test.measure: count of repeat lateness incidents on the same task

title: Write and own a check-in cadence, but choose its length and interval with the human
hypothesis: If a written, owned check-in cadence exists for the team while operating artefacts follow the sourced interval defaults (weekly, fortnightly or monthly), then staleness stops costing stock and cash while the team's own meeting rhythm still matches its real appetite for process, because one source refuses a fixed ratio for team check-ins while another gives fixed intervals for artefacts.

signal.check: No cadence for team check-ins is written down, or an operating artefact has no review interval at all.

expected_effect.size: unknown; sources disagree on team cadence, agree operating artefacts need one

risk.note: A cadence decision, adjustable with the human.

steps: List every operating artefact and set its review interval to weekly, fortnightly or monthly, since staleness has a real cost.
Discuss with the human what check-in interval the team actually wants for its own health conversations.
Write the chosen interval down and name who owns keeping it.
Avoid converting the team's own interval into a rigid universal rule.

test.method: Not a split test; a documentation coverage check.
test.measure: share of artefacts and team check-ins with a written, owned cadence

title: Run 4 meeting types at a small-brand length: annual reset, quarterly deep dive, weekly trading review, ad hoc
hypothesis: If the store keeps the 4 meeting types, annual, quarterly, weekly, ad hoc, but compresses their length for a small team (a half-day quarterly, a 30 to 45 minute weekly), then the team gets the same coverage without spending the fable's full days on it, because the types matter more than their exact duration.

signal.check: The team runs only 1 recurring call type for everything, with no separate quarterly or annual reset.

risk.note: A calendar restructure.

steps: Set an annual reset meeting, shortened to fit a small team.
Set a quarterly deep-dive meeting, such as a half day.
Keep a weekly trading review, 30 to 45 minutes.
Add ad hoc topical meetings as needed, not on a fixed schedule.

test.method: Track whether each of the 4 types has run in the last quarter.
test.measure: count of the 4 meeting types held in the quarter

expected_effect.size: unknown; 1 fictional company's model, small-brand lengths are a pass 1 adaptation

title: Run the weekly meeting on the jugular numbers, and cancel it when there is nothing to debate
hypothesis: If the weekly meeting opens on conversion, stockouts and CS backlog with no laptops, and gets cancelled outright when there is nothing worth debating, then the meeting stops becoming a status report nobody needs, because a meeting held out of habit wastes the exact attention it should be protecting.

signal.check: The weekly meeting runs every week regardless of content, often as a status round with people on laptops.

expected_effect.size: unknown; 2 sources agree, no measured lift given

risk.note: A meeting-format change.

steps: Open every weekly meeting on conversion, stockouts and CS backlog, not a status round.
Set the norm: be present, no laptops.
Pre-circulate the 5 topics that matter before the meeting.
End each meeting with at least 1 decision logged.
If nothing is worth debating that week, cancel the meeting.

test.method: Track the count of logged decisions per weekly meeting and how often it gets cancelled for lack of content.
test.measure: decisions logged per meeting

title: Observe for 2 weeks before changing anything when a new lead takes over a function
hypothesis: If a new ops lead, head of growth or agency spends 2 weeks in the trading meeting, the CS queue and the PO review before touching the promo calendar or the ad account, then their first changes target the real problem, because acting before observing risks fixing the wrong thing.

signal.check: A new leader is about to make changes to process or strategy within their first days on the job.

expected_effect.size: unknown; 1 fable case

risk.note: A short delay before changes, easily explained to the team.

steps: Tell the new leader to spend 2 weeks observing the trading meeting, the CS queue and the PO review.
Ask them to hold silent one-on-ones with the team during this period.
Have them write down what they would change, without acting on it yet.
After 2 weeks, review the list together before any change starts.

test.method: Compare the quality of first changes made after a 2-week observation period vs immediate changes.
test.measure: qualitative fit of the first change to the real problem
test.read_point: 1 month after the new leader starts

title: Handle a missed reorder or a 3PL escalation face to face, never by email or chat
hypothesis: If a missed reorder, a lost test budget, or a 3PL escalation gone wrong gets handled face to face or on a call instead of by email or chat, then the issue gets resolved with less misunderstanding, because a written channel strips out tone and invites delay on exactly the moments that need immediate, direct handling.

signal.check: A serious operational miss is being handled entirely over email or chat.

expected_effect.size: unknown; 2 sources agree on the approach, no measured lift given

risk.note: A communication-channel rule.

steps: When a moment of truth happens, a missed reorder, a lost budget, a bad 3PL escalation, schedule a call or in-person conversation.
Avoid resolving it over email or chat alone.
For a recurring interpersonal conflict behind it, define the problem with the person and develop options together rather than issuing a verdict.

test.method: Track time to resolution and repeat-incident rate for moments handled face to face vs by written channel.
test.measure: resolution time and repeat-incident rate

title: Treat personality instruments as self-disclosure only, not a hiring or fit diagnostic
hypothesis: If MBTI or similar instruments are used only for self-disclosure and team conversation, never as a serious diagnostic for hiring or fit decisions, then the team avoids over-trusting a contested tool, because MBTI's reliability and validity are widely disputed outside the source's own framing.
does_not_apply_when: the instrument is used only as an icebreaker or discussion prompt

signal.check: A personality instrument's result is being used to justify a hiring, promotion or role-fit decision.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a caution, not a measured effect

risk.note: A policy on how to use an existing tool, not a new cost.

steps: Check the current standing and validity critique of MBTI before recommending it to a client or team.
Use any personality instrument only as a conversation starter, never as a hire or fit decision input.
Where a conflict-mode choice matters, choose the mode deliberately rather than defaulting to habit.

test.method: Not a split test; a policy audit of where the instrument's results get used.
test.measure: whether the instrument influences any hire, pay or promotion decision
test.read_point: At each use of the instrument

title: Skip ropes-course and outdoor team-building as a standalone trust fix
hypothesis: If outdoor or experiential exercises are used only on top of the fundamental trust, conflict and accountability tools and only for a named skill gap, then the store avoids spending on an activity whose benefits often do not translate back to work, because 1 source explicitly says these exercises have lost their shine for a reason.
does_not_apply_when: the human specifically wants an outdoor event and the fundamentals are already in place

signal.check: An outdoor or ropes-course event is being proposed as the fix for a trust problem, with no fundamental tools run first.

expected_effect.size: unknown; 1 source calls the gains from such exercises inconsistent

risk.note: Avoids a discretionary spend rather than adding one.

steps: Run the fundamental tools first: the team assessment (P5) and the scoreboard process (P9).
Only propose an outdoor or skills workshop for a specifically named skill gap, such as listening or role clarity.
Never present it as the trust fix on its own.

test.method: Not a split test; a spend-decision filter.
test.measure: whether a named skill gap exists before any outdoor event is booked

title: Judge a launch team by whether the drop shipped and sold through, not by the meeting's mood
hypothesis: If a launch or seasonal drop team is judged on whether it shipped on time and sold through, and only secondarily on the meeting's atmosphere, then the team stops mistaking a pleasant meeting for a successful launch, because a relaxed room can still miss the deadline.

signal.check: A launch retrospective focuses only on how the meetings felt, with no reference to ship date or sell-through.

expected_effect.size: unknown; 1 source's 12 signs are a checklist, not a measured lift

risk.note: A retrospective format change.

steps: After every launch, record whether it shipped on time and its early sell-through.
Separately score the 12 team-process signs, such as open expression and conflict on ideas not personalities, as a secondary read.
Compare the 2 sets side by side rather than substituting one for the other.
Use the process signs only to explain a result, never to override it.

test.method: Track launch on-time rate and sell-through against the process-sign score over several launches.
test.measure: launch_on_time_rate and other:sell_through_at_2_weeks

title: Check communication, structural and personal causes when a launch team underperforms
hypothesis: If a poor launch or ops team result gets checked against communication, structural and personal causes, and against the external system, selection, rewards, training, that existed before the team formed, then the real fix targets the actual cause instead of blaming the people in the room.

signal.check: A launch squad or ops team performs badly and the review blames only the people, without checking structure or the system around them.

expected_effect.size: unknown; 1 source's categories, no measured lift given

risk.note: A retrospective checklist addition.

steps: Check communication causes: listening, information sharing, interpretation, nonverbal signals.
Check structural causes: team size, turnover, participation, rewards, interdependence.
Check personal causes: self-esteem, goals, values.
Check the external system that existed before the team formed: selection, culture, training, rewards.
Look for failure signs: resource resentment, cost overruns, slipped dates, unclear responsibilities, lost focus.

test.method: Run the checklist on the next underperforming launch and compare the identified cause to the fix applied.
test.measure: whether the fix matches the identified cause category

title: Match communication method to work type: live meetings for interdependent work, dashboards for routine work
hypothesis: If routine, autonomous work like daily stock counts moves to a dashboard while emerging, interdependent work like a replan after a competitor price cut gets a live trading meeting, then reporting sludge drops and real decisions still get the live discussion they need, because over-reporting on easy technology causes people to disengage from what actually matters.

signal.check: Routine work gets discussed live in meetings, or interdependent, emerging work is buried in a report nobody reads.

expected_effect.size: unknown; 1 source's matrix, no measured lift given

risk.note: A communication-channel reassignment.

steps: List recurring work items and classify each as routine or emerging, autonomous or interdependent.
Move routine, autonomous work, such as daily stock counts, to a dashboard.
Keep emerging, interdependent work, such as a competitor-driven replan, in a live meeting.
Cut any report nobody reads or acts on.

test.method: Count reports produced but not opened or acted on before and after the reassignment.
test.measure: other:unused_report_count

title: Free a meeting the founder dominates by stepping out or giving quiet members a turn
hypothesis: If the founder talks less, uses a turn-taking device such as a fixed number of talk turns, or steps out so the group can work, then the ops and CS owners start speaking up in the trading meeting, because a dominated meeting hides exactly the information those owners hold.

signal.check: The founder talks most of the trading meeting and the ops and CS owners rarely speak.

expected_effect.size: unknown; 1 anecdote reports a large shift, not a typical figure

risk.note: A facilitation technique.

steps: Track roughly who speaks and for how long in the next few trading meetings.
If 1 or 2 people dominate, use a fixed number of talk turns, such as poker chips, to limit them.
Hold silence deliberately so a quiet member fills it.
For a persistently dominated meeting, have the founder step out so the group can work.

test.method: Track talk-share balance before and after the intervention.
test.measure: other:meeting_talk_share_balance

title: Run the weekly accountability review on the overarching goal's named drivers, not status updates
