hypothesis: If the weekly review opens on the overarching goal, decomposes it into a short list of named drivers each with 1 owner and 1 date, and closes each driver with a decision or reassignment, then the team stays focused on what actually moves the goal, because status updates with no decision waste the meeting's real value.

signal.check: The weekly review is a round of status updates with no reference to the overarching goal's drivers.

expected_effect.size: unknown; 1 source, fable-based procedure

risk.note: A meeting-agenda format change.

steps: Open the meeting on the overarching goal.
Decompose it into a short list of named drivers, each with 1 owner and 1 date.
Have each owner report ahead or behind without spin.
When an owner blames someone else's slowness, ask them to name the blocker and treat their failure to escalate earlier as the issue.
Push with respect on every owner, including the leader.
Close each driver with a decision or a reassignment; the next meeting starts from the same list.
Reserve the last 10 minutes for cascading messaging.

test.method: Track the share of drivers closed with a decision each week vs left open.
test.measure: other:driver_closure_rate

title: Map Belbin-style behaviour roles to a seasonal launch team, and flag a team stacked with only implementers
hypothesis: If a seasonal launch team is staffed by observed behaviour, merchandising leaning coordinator and implementer, creative leaning plant, margin review leaning monitor evaluator, supplier relations leaning resource investigator, site QA leaning completer, then the team stops being stacked with only 1 behaviour type, because a team of all implementers executes but never questions the plan.

signal.check: A launch team is being staffed by title or availability, not by observed behaviour, or every member behaves the same way in meetings.

expected_effect.size: unknown; 1 source, pass 1 mapping to store functions

risk.note: A staffing check, not a hire.

prerequisites: observed behaviours for each team member
steps: Before staffing the next launch team, note each candidate's observed behaviour, not their title.
Check the team includes a coordinator-type, a plant-type (idea generator) and a monitor-evaluator-type (critical reviewer).
Flag a team where everyone behaves like an implementer, since it will execute but rarely question the plan.
Adjust the roster or explicitly assign someone to play the missing behaviour for this launch.

test.method: Compare launch outcomes for teams checked against this mix vs teams staffed by availability alone.
test.measure: other:launch_on_time_rate and count of issues caught before launch

title: Staff both task roles and process roles instead of the founder holding every role out of busyness
hypothesis: If a team names both the task roles, who does the work, and the process roles, who keeps the group working well together, instead of the founder defaulting to holding every role, then meetings and launches run better, because busyness is not a reason to skip naming who manages the group's process.

signal.check: The founder holds every process role, such as facilitator and timekeeper, by default because 'nobody else has time'.

expected_effect.size: unknown; 1 source

risk.note: A role reassignment within an existing team.

steps: List task roles (who executes) and process roles (who facilitates, keeps time, checks in on the group) separately.
Assign at least 1 process role to someone other than the founder.
Rotate process roles across meetings to avoid 1 person defaulting to all of them.

test.method: Not a split test; a role-assignment check.
test.measure: share of process roles held by someone other than the founder

title: Write a 1-R responsibility chart naming exactly 1 owner per recurring decision type
hypothesis: If price changes, promotions, site changes, PO releases, 3PL escalations, refund exceptions and hire requests each get exactly 1 R (the person who initiates and ensures it is done) on a published chart, then decisions stop stalling on unclear ownership, because 4 separate sources all converge on naming exactly 1 owner per decision.

signal.check: A recurring decision type has 0 or more than 1 person who could claim ownership, or no chart exists at all.

expected_effect.size: unknown; 4 sources agree on the principle, no measured lift given

risk.note: A documentation exercise.

steps: List decision types down the side: price change, promotion, site change, PO release, 3PL escalation, refund exception, hire request.
List actors across the top.
Fill each cell: R (initiates and ensures done), A-V (approve or veto), S (support), I (inform, cannot influence).
Fix any row with 0 or 2 R values in the meeting where it is found.
Publish the finished chart where the team can see it.

test.method: Track decisions that stall on unclear ownership before and after the chart is published.
test.measure: count of ownership-stalled decisions per month

title: Classify every decision as high stakes or everyday before deciding how much process to use
hypothesis: If a decision gets classified as high stakes, a pricing or offer change, a platform migration, a 3PL switch, a repositioning, a large PO, or as an everyday call before deciding how much process to apply, then the team stops over-processing small calls and under-processing big ones, because 3 sources agree on the split even if they disagree on exactly where the line sits.

signal.check: A decision is being made with no check for whether it is high stakes or reversible.

expected_effect.size: unknown; 3 sources agree on the split, disagree on the exact line

risk.note: A triage step before deciding, not the decision itself.

steps: Before any significant decision, ask whether it is a pricing or offer change, a platform migration, a 3PL switch, a repositioning, or a large PO.
If yes, route it through the full debate process for high-stakes calls.
If no, decide it in the meeting without extended debate.
Speed up for a flash-sale response; slow down when several perspectives, such as ops, finance and growth, are needed.

test.method: Track which decisions went through full debate vs quick call, and whether that matched their actual stakes in hindsight.
test.measure: other:decision_triage_accuracy

title: Frame a high-stakes decision before debating it: exact question, right people, data in advance, who decides
hypothesis: If a high-stakes decision is framed with the exact question, the right people by knowledge, stake and execution, the data in advance, and who decides stated up front, then the debate that follows produces a real decision instead of an opinion contest, because 'we'll just use my opinion' is named as the anti-pattern this framing prevents.

signal.check: A high-stakes discussion starts with no exact question written down, no named decider, and no data prepared in advance.

expected_effect.size: unknown; 1 source

risk.note: A pre-meeting preparation step.

steps: Write the exact question, such as 'raise the hero SKU price 10 percent before peak, yes or no'.
Invite people by knowledge, stake and execution duty, not by seniority alone.
Send the relevant data in advance: margin per SKU, elasticity from past tests, days of stock.
State up front who decides.

test.method: Check whether each element (question, people, data, decider) was in place before the debate started.
test.measure: other:decision_framing_completeness

title: Run high-stakes debates with both safety and rigour at once
hypothesis: If a high-stakes debate has the leader speak last, 1 person assigned to argue the other side, and evidence weighed over hierarchy, then the group avoids settling too early on a decision like a 3PL switch, because safety lets people speak and rigour keeps the group testing the answer instead of just agreeing with the loudest voice.

signal.check: A debate is settling quickly with no dissenting view voiced, or the leader speaks first and sets the room's direction.

expected_effect.size: unknown; 1 source

risk.note: A facilitation technique for the debate itself.

steps: Have the leader speak last in the debate.
Assign 1 person to argue the other side, such as the case for staying with the current 3PL.
Require evidence for both sides and keep asking why.
Do not let the group settle early; weigh evidence over hierarchy.

test.method: Track whether a dissenting view was voiced and considered in each high-stakes debate.
test.measure: other:debate_dissent_rate

title: Log every decision with the metric it should move and a review date
hypothesis: If every closed decision is logged with the store metric it should move and a review date, then the team can check later whether it worked instead of relitigating whether it was decided, because announcing a decision without a clear close leaves people debating its soundness instead of executing it.

signal.check: A decision was made with no written record of the metric it should move or when to check it.

expected_effect.size: unknown; combined from 2 sources, no measured lift given

risk.note: A logging habit.

steps: After closing any decision, write down what was decided, why now, and who decided.
Name the store metric it should move.
Set a review date to check the metric.
Communicate the decision and the reasoning to everyone affected, and let others watch where possible.

test.method: Track whether logged decisions get reviewed on their set date.
test.measure: share of decisions reviewed on schedule

title: Bring planners and full-time staff into the room before a high-stakes inventory or forecasting decision
hypothesis: If the peak PO or a forecast method change gets a full-input debate involving planners and the people who will execute it, instead of a rushed fix by 1 person, then the store avoids the kind of rushed 'band-aid' forecasting decision the source's own case describes replacing with a proper in-season method.

signal.check: A large or unusual PO, or a change to the forecast method, is being decided by 1 person without input from planners or execution staff.

expected_effect.size: unknown; 1 source, 1 case (Lands' End)

risk.note: A process step before a large PO or forecast change.

steps: Before a peak PO or a forecast method change, list who has knowledge, stake and execution duty.
Bring them into the room together rather than deciding with 1 person's view.
Run the full decision-framing and debate process (R82, R83) on the choice.
Document the decision and review date.

test.method: Compare forecast accuracy for decisions made with full input vs decisions made by 1 person alone.
test.measure: forecast miss percent against actual sell-through
test.read_point: After the peak or seasonal window closes

title: Run the full Debate Maker process for every high-stakes store decision
hypothesis: If a high-stakes decision runs through framing, a safety-and-rigour debate, and an explicit close with cascading messaging, then the organisation executes the decision instead of relitigating it, because announcing a decision after collecting opinions without debating them leaves people debating its soundness rather than acting on it.

signal.check: A pricing change, platform migration, 3PL switch, major repositioning or large PO is being decided without a structured framing and debate step.

risk.note: If the decision was announced without debate, expect execution drag; reopen once with the data, then close for good.

steps: Frame: write the exact question; invite people by knowledge, stake and execution; require data in advance; state who decides.
Spark: leader speaks last; assign someone to argue the other side; ask for evidence on both sides; keep asking why; ignore rank when weighing input.
Drive: state whether it is decided now or needs more data; make the call or delegate it explicitly; communicate the decision and reasoning; let others watch where possible.
End with cascading messaging so the same message reaches everyone.

test.method: Track whether the team relitigates the decision in the weeks after it closes.
test.measure: other:decision_execution_drag
test.read_point: 2 to 4 weeks after the decision closes

expected_effect.size: unknown; 1 source, no measured lift given

title: Delegate a whole outcome with 51 percent of the vote, not a slice of a task
hypothesis: If an owner is given a whole outcome, such as the email programme or the reorder review, with real vote and full responsibility, coached with questions rather than answers, then that owner grows into the role faster, because a slice of a task with the leader still holding the pen never produces real ownership.

signal.check: A person is nominally responsible for an outcome, but the leader still makes most of the actual decisions on it.

expected_effect.size: unknown; 1 source, illustrative framework

risk.note: Reset the split out loud if it fails; do not quietly resume control.

steps: Name the owner and state the split: 51 percent of the vote, 100 percent of the responsibility; the leader stays in the loop.
Give the whole outcome, not a slice, and stretch the role 1 level above current comfort.
Coach with questions, not answers; add a second person as a sounding board without moving accountability.
When a problem returns, ask 'what would you like to do to fix this' and never accept a problem without a proposed fix.
If you must grab the pen for a genuine emergency, hand it back before the work is done.
Let natural consequences run; do not rescue.
Put the owner's numbers on a visible scoreboard.

test.method: After 2 weeks, ask who is doing most of the thinking on this work.
test.measure: other:delegation_depth
test.read_point: 2 weeks after the delegation starts, then quarterly

title: Run a 30-day trial of 1 leadership practice instead of trying to fix every habit at once
hypothesis: If a leader picks exactly 1 practice, such as labelling each person's genius in a staff meeting or bringing planners into the forecasting debate, runs it for 30 days with a journal, and judges it by others' behaviour rather than their own effort, then the habit sticks, because trying to develop several disciplines at once is a named common mistake.

signal.check: A leader is trying to change several habits at once, or has no journal or day-30 check planned.

expected_effect.size: unknown; the 30-day figure is the author's assertion, no study named

risk.note: Pick a smaller practice if this one proves too big, not a second one at the same time.

steps: Rate yourself on the leadership disciplines, formally or informally.
Pick the single weakest and single strongest.
Choose exactly 1 practice inside 1 discipline to change for 30 days, such as labelling a team member's strength publicly or holding silence for a quiet member.
Journal daily for 30 days.
At day 30, judge by others' behaviour, not your own effort.
Add the next layer only after this one holds, and find a peer partner for the following year's question.

test.method: Check journal entries and ask the team whether the behaviour change is visible.
test.measure: other:habit_change_completion and journal entries out of 30 days

title: Run a private capability-gap check with each key person before opening a hire
hypothesis: If each key person is privately asked to estimate what percent of their capability their current manager gets, and an assumption audit and ownership check are run alongside it, then a hidden underuse problem surfaces before a hire is opened, because 40 to 60 percent or lower is a self-reported underuse signal worth investigating first.

signal.check: No capability check has been run with key people before a hire request goes forward.

expected_effect.size: self-reported, retrospective; 40 to 60 percent or lower flagged as underuse

risk.note: Answers stay private and are never used for pay decisions.

steps: Privately ask each key person to estimate the percent of their capability their current manager gets, and compare to a past manager.
Run an assumption audit: before a delegation, write how you would handle it under 'they will never figure it out' vs 'they will figure it out', and note which you did.
Run a tense vs intense check after the next hard meeting.
Run an ownership check: are returned problems solved by you, or returned with a question.
If gaps show up, run the 30-day practice change before opening the hire.

test.method: Compare self-reported capability use before and after a leadership practice change.
test.measure: other:reported_capability_utilization
test.read_point: Before the hire decision, then again after 1 quarter of practice change

title: Communicate a senior departure with a plain reason and a same-day interim owner
hypothesis: If a senior departure is announced to the leadership team first, with a plain reason and a named interim owner the same day, then rumours and morale damage stay contained, because unanswered practical questions, how they took it, the interim plan, what gets said outside, are what create anxiety.

signal.check: A senior person is leaving and no interim owner or communication plan has been prepared.

expected_effect.size: unknown; 1 source, fable-based procedure

risk.note: A departure cannot be undone; the communication plan is what is reversible in how it lands.

steps: Tell the leadership team first and say some detail stays confidential.
Give the plain reason, such as unwillingness to change behaviour that hurt the team.
Answer the practical questions: how they took it, the interim plan, what employees and press will hear.
Name the interim owner of the function the same day and state confidence in the plan.
Use 1 simple external line, such as 'moving on'.
Open the conversation about how the team feels and expect mourning or self-doubt even after a deserved exit.

test.method: Track handoff quality and team morale in the 2 weeks after the announcement.
test.measure: other:post_departure_disruption

title: Give every operating artefact 1 named owner and a fixed update cadence
hypothesis: If every operating artefact, the tech pack, critical path, PO tracker, forecast, 3PL SLA, CS routing rules, gets 1 named owner and a fixed cadence, then stale data stops propagating into other teams' decisions, because 'I'll update it later' on a shared sheet is the top named failure.

signal.check: Any artefact has no named owner, or its last update is older than its stated cadence.

expected_effect.size: unknown; 2 sources agree, no measured lift given

risk.note: A documentation exercise.

steps: List every operating artefact.
Assign 1 named owner and 1 update cadence to each.
Have the owner state target and result at every review.
Flag any artefact past its cadence as a capacity risk.

test.method: Check last-updated dates against the stated cadence for every artefact.
test.measure: share of artefacts updated within their cadence

title: Never release a large purchase order without a tech pack on file
hypothesis: If no large PO goes out without a tech pack on file, then a quality or IP dispute with a supplier has an evidence base to stand on, because the tech pack is what let 1 brand prove a fabric substitution against the GSM spec and get replacements.

signal.check: A large PO is about to go out with no tech pack on file for the product.

expected_effect.size: unknown; 1 anecdote, no percent given

risk.note: A gate before spend commits; check current freelance pricing before commissioning one.

steps: Check whether a tech pack exists for the product before releasing the PO.
If the team cannot write one, commission a freelancer with a defined deliverable.
File the tech pack where it can be referenced in any future quality or IP dispute.
Route the tech pack's full contents list and supplier negotiation detail to sourcing.

test.method: Track quality disputes with and without a tech pack on file.
test.measure: defect_rate and count of unresolved quality disputes

title: Pick 1 lever per SKU when negotiating a supplier quote: low MOQ, low price, or short lead time
hypothesis: If the PO owner picks 1 lever per SKU, low MOQ for a small budget, low price for margin, or short lead time for cash turns, and compares at least 2 factories, then negotiation stays realistic, because a supplier rarely gives all 3 levers at once.

signal.check: A supplier quote has no volume tiers and no comparison against a second factory.

expected_effect.size: unknown; 1 source, no percent for this specific choice

risk.note: A negotiation decision, revisited at the next order.

steps: For each SKU, decide which lever matters most: MOQ, price, or lead time.
For a wide catalogue, lean toward low MOQ per colour and size; for a hero SKU with steady sell-through, lean toward price.
Compare at least 2 factories before committing.
Check landed cost against the intended retail price before signing.

test.method: Compare landed cost and cash-cycle impact across the chosen lever vs the prior order.
test.measure: landed_cost and cash_conversion_days

title: Run a critical path with 1 owner and 1 date per production step, and never give suppliers edit access
hypothesis: If every production step from strike-off to inbound has 1 named owner and 1 date worked back from the hard deadline, monitored daily, with suppliers holding view-only access, then a seasonal window stops getting missed by a slipped, unowned step, because a supplier who can edit the shared timeline can quietly move the very date the store is depending on.

signal.check: The critical path has steps with no named owner or no date, or a supplier has edit access to it.

expected_effect.size: unknown; 1 source, example durations only

risk.note: If the path cannot reach the deadline, decide early to skip the window rather than land stock late.

steps: List every step: strike-offs, first sample, revised sample, production sample, QC, bulk, freight, inbound.
Assign a duration per step using past examples as a guide.
Set dates back from the hard deadline.
Assign 1 owner per step.
Monitor daily with overdue reminders; push downstream dates or use slack when a step slips.
Give suppliers view-only access, never edit access.
Check the inbound date lands before the PDP goes live.

test.method: Track whether each critical path step lands on its set date.
test.measure: other:critical_path_on_time_rate
test.read_point: At the end of each production cycle

title: Build the demand forecast base by excluding stockout days and using a trend or seasonal curve
hypothesis: If the forecast base excludes stockout days and uses a month-on-month trend for under a year of history or a month-by-month seasonal curve where about 90 to 95 percent of ecommerce has meaningful seasonality, then the reorder quantity reflects real demand, because a base period padded with zero-stock days understates true demand and drives under-ordering.

signal.check: The forecast base period includes stockout days, or a seasonal category is forecast with a flat monthly average.

expected_effect.size: unknown; single-operator heuristic, own growing-brand forecast miss estimate about 50 percent

risk.note: If the forecast misses by about 50 percent, re-check the base period before changing the growth assumption.

prerequisites: sales by day with stockout days flagged
steps: Exclude stockout days from the base period; if 15 of 30 days were in stock, extrapolate from the 15.
Under a year of history or during fast growth, use a month-on-month trend.
If seasonality dominates the category, build a month-by-month curve and check product seasonality on a trend tool.
For a wide catalogue, forecast at colour and size level, not product level, since each variant sells its own curve.

test.method: Compare forecast accuracy for periods using the corrected base vs the old method.
test.measure: forecast miss percent against actual sell-through

title: Set a days-of-stock target by volatility and capital, and add safety stock only after padding lead time
hypothesis: If days of stock is set to 4, 8 or 12 weeks by volatility and available cash, manufacturing lead time is padded with an average rather than a best case, and 5 to 10 days of safety stock is added only after that padding, then both stockouts and cash locked in excess inventory drop, because both under-ordering and over-ordering are existential for a small store's cash.

signal.check: The days-of-stock target and safety stock were set with no reference to lead time padding, or a range extension is being approved with no cash-tied-up check.

expected_effect.size: heuristic: 4, 8 or 12 weeks by volatility and capital; safety stock 5 to 10 days

risk.note: Both too little and too much stock are existential for cash; check with the human on cash available before setting the target.

steps: Enter manufacturing lead time, not shipping time, padded with the average.
Set days of stock at 4, 8 or 12 weeks based on demand volatility and available capital.
Add 5 to 10 days of safety stock only after the lead time is padded.
Before approving a new colour or size, check the days of stock and cash tied up it would add.
Read the sell-out date and recommended reorder quantity.

test.method: Track stockout days and cash tied up in inventory over 2 to 3 reorder cycles.
test.measure: stockout_days and days_of_stock

title: Keep 1 authoritative PO copy in accounting software and 1 team-visible tracker, internal only
hypothesis: If the store keeps 1 authoritative PO copy in accounting software and 1 team-visible tracker with SKU, quantity, dates and shipping detail, checked before any discontinuation or mass refund, then finance, ops, marketing and CS stop working from stale or conflicting PO data, because each function reads the same numbers to pause ads, update a pre-order macro, or plan a reorder.

signal.check: POs live only as order lines in a supplier platform, with no team-visible tracker, or a product is being discontinued without checking the PO tracker first.

expected_effect.size: unknown; 1 source, no measured lift given

risk.note: A documentation and process change.

steps: Raise every formal PO with product, price, quantity, ship-to and terms.
Keep the authoritative copy in accounting software.
Keep a team-visible tracker with SKU, quantity, PO number, departure date, ETA, vessel or air tracking.
Push every ETA change to the team channel.
Check the tracker before discontinuing a product or issuing mass refunds.
From about $5M to $10M revenue, assign a dedicated tracker owner; from about $30M to $50M, consider an ERP.

test.method: Audit tracker last-updated date against actual ETA changes.
test.measure: other:po_tracker_staleness_days

title: Re-shop freight providers monthly and compare 2 to 3 at a time
hypothesis: If freight providers are compared 2 to 3 at a time and re-shopped monthly, preferring providers in the store's own region, then freight cost stays competitive, because rates and service change often enough that a locked-in provider can quietly drift out of line with the market.

signal.check: The store has used the same freight provider for months with no re-shop or comparison.

expected_effect.size: unknown; 1 source, no percent given for freight specifically

risk.note: A comparison exercise, no commitment change until a decision is made.

steps: List current freight providers and cost per shipment.
Each month, request quotes from 2 to 3 providers, preferring ones in the store's own region.
Compare against the current provider's rate.
Switch or renegotiate if a meaningfully better rate or service is found.

test.method: Track freight cost per unit across re-shop cycles.
test.measure: other:freight_cost_per_unit

title: Choose a 3PL by competitive RFP with a facility visit, never on 1 quote or price alone
hypothesis: If a 3PL is chosen by sending an identical RFP, including the real growth forecast, to several providers and visiting or seeing interior footage of each facility, then the store avoids picking a 3PL that fails during peak, because the source's own case shows a 3PL that could not ship during an October to November peak cost over $20M in lost revenue.

signal.check: A 3PL is being chosen or reviewed based on 1 quote, price alone, or no facility visit.

expected_effect.size: 1 source's case: over $20M lost against a $45M to $50M peak forecast from a single 3PL failure

risk.note: Keep a second qualified 3PL from the RFP on file in case of failure.

prerequisites: growth forecast the brand intends to hit
steps: Build a master RFP with dimensions, order history and the real growth forecast.
Send the identical RFP to several 3PLs.
Visit each facility or review interior footage; treat a refusal as a red flag.
Confirm barcode scanning inbound and outbound.
Price pick and pack, inbound, outbound and storage separately across all quotes.
Judge whether you will be a valued account, not their smallest or largest client.
Give every 3PL an honest forecast, not an inflated one.
Keep the RFP runner-up warm as a backup.

test.method: Track on-time ship rate and pick time after switching to the selected 3PL.
test.measure: on_time_ship_rate

title: Put the 3PL SLA in writing with a pick-time clause and a stated consequence for a miss
hypothesis: If the 3PL SLA is written with pick time of 24 to 48 hours off-peak, a stated consequence for a missed pick, delivered-on-time language, at least 2 cycle counts a year, and ASN and booking rules, then the store has grounds to enforce service standards, because 3PLs will not put delivered-on-time in the SLA unless the store asks for it explicitly.

signal.check: The current 3PL relationship runs on a verbal understanding, or the SLA has no consequence clause for a missed pick.

expected_effect.size: unknown; 1 source's recommendation, no measured lift given

risk.note: Agree the peak pick-time clause before the peak forecast is sent.

steps: Write pick time as 24 to 48 hours off-peak into the SLA.
State a consequence for a missed pick, such as a discount or a free pick.
Include delivered-on-time language, at least 2 cycle counts a year, and ASN and booking rules.
Sign the SLA before the first inbound shipment.

test.method: Track pick time and delivered-on-time rate against the written SLA terms.
test.measure: on_time_ship_rate

title: Track delivered-on-time yourself and split pick lag from carrier lag before claiming a credit
hypothesis: If the store tracks delivered-on-time itself and separates pick-time lag from carrier lag before asking the 3PL for a refund, then complaints about slow delivery get resolved with real evidence, because a 3PL will not track this for the store and a rise in 'where is my order' tickets can come from either side.

signal.check: Where-is-my-order tickets are rising and delivered-on-time is below about 95 percent, with no internal tracking of the cause.

expected_effect.size: threshold: investigate below about 95 percent

risk.note: Show the metric as unavailable, never 0, when the data is missing.

steps: Track delivered-on-time using the store's own data, not the 3PL's report.
When it falls below about 95 percent, split pick-time lag from carrier lag before acting.
Escalate to the 3PL with the specific cause identified.
Ask for a credit only once the cause is isolated.

test.method: Compare delivered-on-time before and after isolating the cause and escalating.
test.measure: on_time_ship_rate

title: Audit every monthly 3PL invoice against your own order volume in code
hypothesis: If the store rebuilds expected pick and pack, inbound, outbound and storage cost from its own Shopify order count each month and compares it line by line to the 3PL invoice, then overcharges get caught, because 1 source's client sample found 30 to 40 percent of invoices had some overcharge.

signal.check: 3PL invoices are paid without comparing them to expected cost from the store's own order data.

expected_effect.size: unverified client-sample claim: 30 to 40 percent of one sample overcharged somewhere

risk.note: A reconciliation process; missing data shows as unavailable, never 0.

steps: Each month, pull Shopify order count, units, inbound receipts and pallets stored.
Compute expected pick and pack, inbound, outbound and storage cost from the SLA rate card, in code.
Compare to the invoice line by line and flag any line above expected.
Pull delivered-on-time and pick time alongside the invoice check.
If delivered-on-time is under about 95 percent, separate pick lag from carrier lag before disputing a charge.

test.method: Track disputed charges and dollars recovered per month.
test.measure: other:invoice_overcharge_rate and dollars disputed

title: Staff CS tiers from the sales forecast curve and track cost per ticket monthly
hypothesis: If simple, repeatable tickets route to 1 tier and complex or escalated ones to another, with hiring and training timed from the sales forecast curve rather than current ticket volume, and cost per ticket tracked monthly, then CS scales ahead of a peak instead of behind it, because a rising cost per ticket while tickets rise signals headcount or routing already lags.

signal.check: CS hiring or training is planned from current ticket volume, not the sales forecast, or cost per ticket is not tracked.

expected_effect.size: unknown; single-operator claim that local agents are about 2x as efficient untrained, no percent on cost overall

risk.note: A staffing and reporting change.

steps: Define 'complex' ticket in writing.
Route simple, repeatable tickets (order status, return labels) to 1 tier and complex or escalated ones (a damaged high-AOV order, a chargeback) to another.
Do not assume 1 tier is cheaper without accounting for training and macros.
Plan hiring and training dates from the sales forecast curve, not current ticket volume.
Compute cost per ticket monthly as (software plus agents) divided by tickets.
If cost per ticket rises while tickets rise, treat it as a sign headcount or routing lags.

test.method: Track cost per ticket and ticket backlog through the next peak.
test.measure: other:cost_per_ticket and ticket_backlog
test.read_point: Monthly, and through the next peak

title: Staff a pre-purchase CS lane for a considered or high-AOV product
hypothesis: If a considered or high-AOV product gets a staffed pre-purchase support lane, someone who knows the product answering questions before checkout, then checkout completion improves, because a confused mind says no and pre-purchase CS exists specifically to clear that confusion.

signal.check: Pre-purchase questions go unanswered or route through the same queue as post-purchase tickets, with no dedicated pre-purchase coverage.

expected_effect.size: unknown; 1 source, opinion with no data

risk.note: A staffing and routing change; reversible if it does not move conversion.

steps: Identify the products where purchase is considered or AOV is high.
Staff a pre-purchase lane, live chat or a fast-response channel, with someone who knows the product.
Route pre-purchase questions here separately from post-purchase tickets.
Track checkout completion for sessions that used the lane vs those that did not.

test.method: Compare checkout completion rate for sessions that used pre-purchase support vs those that did not.
test.measure: cvr_checkout_to_order
test.read_point: After 4 to 6 weeks of the staffed lane running

title: Trace a rising resolution time upstream before blaming CS agents
hypothesis: If a slow resolution time or a falling review score gets traced upstream, missing internal information, slow systems, weak macros, then PO accuracy and freight and pick time, before blaming support agents, then the real fix targets the actual cause, because reviews and resolution time are lagging outputs of the rest of operations.

signal.check: Reviews or resolution time are declining and the fix under discussion is only 'hire more CS agents' or 'retrain the team'.

expected_effect.size: unknown; 1 source, diagnostic order not a measured lift

risk.note: A diagnostic step before spending on a CS fix.

steps: Check for missing internal information, such as no ETA in the tracker, first.
Check for slow agents or systems, then weak macros.
Check PO accuracy, then freight and 3PL pick time.
Only after these are ruled out, treat it as a CS staffing or training problem.

test.method: Run the diagnostic order on the next resolution-time spike and record which layer was the actual cause.
test.measure: which diagnostic layer was the true cause

title: Match operations tooling to revenue stage instead of buying an ERP too early
hypothesis: If the store runs on a spreadsheet plus accounting software until about $30M to $50M revenue, adds a dedicated tracker owner at about $5M to $10M, and only then considers an ERP, then the store avoids a costly early ERP purchase, because the source's own case quotes ERP implementation cost from over $200,000 to upward of half a million dollars.
does_not_apply_when: the tracker is stale despite having a dedicated owner, which points to a process problem, not a tooling gap

signal.check: An ERP purchase is being pitched well below about $30M to $50M revenue, or the tracker is stale despite already having a dedicated owner.

expected_effect.size: single-operator figures: ERP cost 'over $200,000', own case 'upward of half a million'

risk.note: An ERP purchase is a large, hard-to-reverse spend; check current pricing and features before committing.

steps: Confirm current revenue against the stage thresholds.
Below about $5M to $10M, run on spreadsheet plus accounting software.
At about $5M to $10M, assign a dedicated tracker owner rather than buying new software.
Only at about $30M to $50M, evaluate an ERP, checking current pricing and the roughly 90 percent coordination it claims to absorb.
If the tracker is stale despite an owner, treat it as a process problem before blaming the tool.

test.method: Track tracker staleness and tool spend against revenue stage.
test.measure: other:po_tracker_staleness_days and tooling spend as a percent of revenue

title: Judge any operations change by customer output, cost and process load together
hypothesis: If a new 3PL, helpdesk or forecast tool is judged on delivered-on-time, cost per ticket or days of stock, plus its cost and the owner hours it takes, rather than 1 internal metric alone, then a change that looks good on paper but adds hidden hours does not get adopted, because a tool can improve 1 number while quietly increasing the load on the person running it.

signal.check: A new operations tool or vendor is being evaluated on 1 internal metric alone, with no cost or owner-hours check.

expected_effect.size: unknown; 1 source, evaluation framework not a measured lift

risk.note: An evaluation checklist, not a change itself.

steps: Before adopting a new 3PL, helpdesk or forecast tool, define which customer-facing metric it should move.
Estimate its cost and the owner hours it will take to run.
Compare all 3, output, cost and hours, side by side before deciding.
Review the same 3 after 1 quarter of use.

test.method: Compare the customer-facing metric, cost and owner hours before and after adopting the change.
test.measure: the relevant customer-facing metric, cost, and owner hours

title: Decide make vs buy for fulfilment before running a 3PL RFP
hypothesis: If the store explicitly compares an in-house warehouse against staying with a 3PL, on cost per order, peak capacity and founder hours, before running a 3PL RFP, then the RFP itself only happens once outsourcing is the confirmed direction, because running an RFP without first deciding make vs buy risks optimising the wrong option.

signal.check: Order volume or returns are straining the current setup, or a lease decision is on the table, with no explicit make-vs-buy comparison done yet.

expected_effect.size: unknown; no library source compares in-house vs 3PL directly, verify against brand data

risk.note: A warehouse lease or a 3PL exit is hard to reverse quickly; decide with real cost data.

steps: Compare cost per order for in-house fulfilment vs staying with a 3PL.
Compare peak capacity under each option.
Compare the founder or ops hours each option takes.
Decide the direction before running the 3PL RFP (if outsourcing wins).

test.method: Not a split test; a 1-time comparison before a structural fulfilment decision.
test.measure: cost per order, peak capacity and owner hours under each option

title: Split traffic from conversion before buying a CRO agency, a media buyer or a redesign
hypothesis: If growth being limited gets split into 'are people reaching the site' and 'are they converting once there' before any fix is bought, then the store stops spending on the wrong side of the funnel, because a plateau or a request for a CRO agency, a media buyer or a redesign is exactly the moment this split gets skipped.

signal.check: A plateau or a request for a CRO agency, media buyer, or redesign is being discussed with no traffic-vs-conversion split done yet.

expected_effect.size: unknown; 1 source, diagnostic framing not a measured lift

risk.note: A diagnostic step before spend commits.

steps: Ask what limits growth: traffic reaching the site, or conversion once there.
Pull sessions and conversion rate by source before proposing any fix.
Do not approve a CRO agency, media buyer or redesign until this split is done.
Route the answer to the correct fix: targeting for a traffic match problem, site work for a conversion problem.

test.method: Track whether the chosen fix (traffic or site) matches which side the data actually showed as weak.
test.measure: other:growth_diagnosis_accuracy
test.read_point: Before any growth spend is approved

title: Segment conversion by source, campaign and geo before running any CRO project
hypothesis: If conversion is segmented by source, campaign and geo before a CRO project starts, then the store fixes the right side of the funnel, because a uniformly low rate points to a site problem while a few sources dragging the average points to a traffic-match problem, and acting on the blended number alone risks the wrong fix.

signal.check: A CRO project or a targeting change is being proposed based on the blended conversion rate alone.

expected_effect.size: unknown; conflicting advice from 2 sources, resolved by segmenting first

risk.note: A diagnostic step, not a change itself.

prerequisites: conversion rate by traffic source, campaign and geo
steps: Pull conversion rate by source, campaign and geo.
If a few sources or geos convert near 0 while others are normal, treat it as a traffic match problem and fix targeting first.
If conversion is uniformly low across sources, treat it as a site problem and run a leaky-bucket audit from landing to checkout.
For a mobile-first market, check mobile vs desktop as a segment before geo.
Never act on the blended conversion rate alone.

test.method: Compare segmented conversion rates before and after the chosen fix (targeting or site).
test.measure: cvr_overall by segment
test.read_point: 4 to 6 weeks after the fix is applied

title: Confirm the founder's strong side with evidence before hiring against the hedged side
hypothesis: If the founder's claimed strong side, such as sourcing, gets confirmed with real evidence, like a favourable buy-to-sell margin on a specific item type, before hiring against the hedged side, then the hire targets a real gap rather than a founder's mistaken self-assessment, because a founder can hedge on a side they are actually strong in.

signal.check: The founder claims a strong side with no evidence pulled to confirm it, at a growth plateau.

expected_effect.size: unknown; 1 source, 1 case

risk.note: A confirmation step before a hiring decision.

steps: Ask the founder which core function they own, sourcing and product or media and acquisition.
Pull real evidence for the claimed strong side, such as buy and sell margin per item.
Note hedging on the other side as a weak, not conclusive, signal.
Confirm the gap with data before finalising the hire target.

test.method: Compare the founder's self-reported strength against the pulled evidence.
test.measure: gross_margin or roas_blended on the claimed strong side
test.read_point: Before the hire decision is finalised

title: Do not treat a sourcing edge as a permanent moat
hypothesis: If margin built on 1 exclusive supplier deal is treated as a short-term edge rather than a permanent moat, then the store plans a follow-up move, brand, list, or repeat base, before competitors find the same supply, because a sourcing edge erodes as competitors find the same deal.

signal.check: Margin is built on 1 supplier deal with no email list or repeat customer base behind it.

expected_effect.size: unknown; 1 source, no measured lift given

risk.note: A strategic planning check, not an immediate operational change.

steps: Identify whether current margin depends mainly on 1 supplier deal.
Check whether a list, repeat base or brand asset exists behind that margin.
If not, plan investment in retention or brand before the supply edge erodes.
Re-check the sourcing edge's exclusivity each quarter.

test.method: Track gross margin and repeat rate as the sourcing edge ages.
test.measure: gross_margin and repeat_rate_90d

title: For a first-mover product, fix acquisition and revenue before investing in brand
hypothesis: If a first-mover, less differentiated product fixes acquisition and revenue first and brand work second, then early cash and growth come faster, because a more differentiated business, such as a luxury or considered purchase, may justify earlier brand investment, but that is not the universal order.
does_not_apply_when: the product is a luxury or considered purchase where differentiation is the main lever

signal.check: A new, first-mover store is investing heavily in brand work before acquisition and revenue are stable.

expected_effect.size: unknown; 1 source, not a universal rule

risk.note: A sequencing decision, not a permanent one.

steps: Check whether the product is a genuine first-mover advantage or a considered, differentiated purchase.
For a first-mover product, prioritise acquisition and revenue work first.
For a considered or luxury purchase, weigh earlier brand investment.
Revisit the sequencing decision once revenue stabilises.

test.method: Track revenue growth under the chosen sequencing over 2 quarters.
test.measure: other:monthly_revenue growth rate

title: Model cash separately from the revenue target before any growth push
hypothesis: If cash is modelled separately from the revenue target before a bigger PO and more ad spend land in the same quarter, then the store avoids the cash strain that arrives right after a growth push, because ecommerce scales fast and over-ordering locks cash exactly when ad spend also needs it.

signal.check: A bigger PO and increased ad spend are both planned for the same quarter with no separate cash model.

expected_effect.size: unknown; 2 sources agree on the risk, no measured lift given

risk.note: A cash shortfall mid-growth-push is hard to reverse quickly; model before committing spend.

steps: Build a 13-week cash view before approving the growth push.
Model the PO and ad spend together against expected revenue timing, not assumed.
Check the model covers inventory and ad spend ahead of the revenue they are meant to produce.
Secure a cash buffer or financing lever before committing to both at once.

test.method: Track actual cash position against the 13-week model through the growth push.
test.measure: cash_conversion_days

title: Fix the PDP or size guide for a recurring pre-purchase question instead of answering it faster
hypothesis: If a recurring pre-purchase question, sizing, shipping time, returns, materials, gets answered on the PDP, in the size guide or at checkout instead of just answering faster in support, then the ticket theme itself drops, because the fix is putting the answer where the shopper already is, not speeding up the reply.

signal.check: The same pre-purchase question theme repeats in tickets, and the fix under discussion is 'answer faster', not a page change.

expected_effect.size: unknown; 1 source, no measured lift given

risk.note: A page content change.

steps: Read tickets for recurring pre-purchase themes: sizing, shipping time, returns, materials.
Put the answer directly on the PDP, in the size guide, or at checkout.
Watch whether the ticket theme volume drops after the page change.
Repeat for the next most common recurring theme.

test.method: Track ticket volume for the specific theme before and after the page change.
test.measure: ticket_backlog for the specific theme

title: Run the full bottleneck diagnosis before funding a hire or a CRO project
hypothesis: If a plateau is diagnosed end to end, traffic vs conversion, segmented conversion, founder archetype, margin against a hire's cost, utilisation, and cash, before any hire or CRO project is funded, then the money goes to the actual constraint, because each step rules out 1 wrong guess before the store commits spend.

signal.check: A hire or CRO project is being proposed to fix a plateau with no structured diagnosis run first.

expected_effect.size: unknown; procedure combines several single-source diagnostics, no combined measured result given

risk.note: A diagnostic procedure before any spend commits.

prerequisites: conversion by source, campaign and geo
steps: Ask what limits growth and split the answer into traffic and conversion.
Pull conversion by source, campaign and geo; do not read the blended number.
If a few sources or geos convert near 0 while others are normal, treat it as a traffic match problem and fix targeting first.
If uniformly low, run the leaky-bucket audit from landing to checkout.
Ask the founder which core function they own; confirm the strong side with evidence; treat the hedged side as the gap.
Check margin against what a hire on the missing side would cost, then run the capability gap check before proposing headcount.
Model cash separately before any growth push.
Output the bottleneck diagnosis naming 1 constraint with the data that shows it.

test.method: Track whether the funded fix (hire, targeting, or site work) matches the diagnosed constraint and whether the target metric moves.
test.measure: the diagnosed constraint's own metric (cvr_overall, roas_blended, or gross_margin)
test.read_point: 1 to 2 quarters after the fix is funded

title: Run the 5-step commitment ladder before rolling out a new cadence, tracker or 3PL
hypothesis: If leadership pictures success out loud, expects a doubt phase, lists unknowns and worst cases, runs a small pilot, and brings the team in through small-group questions before rolling out a new cadence, tracker or 3PL, then real commitment forms instead of people pretending to agree, because a team that only says yes while meaning maybe skipped the support phase.

signal.check: A new direction, cadence, tracker or 3PL, is being announced with no unknowns list, no pilot, and no small-group input gathered first.

expected_effect.size: unknown; 1 source, framework not a measured lift

risk.note: If people pretend to commit, return to the support phase rather than pushing forward.

steps: State a vision bigger than a paycheck and picture success out loud.
Expect a doubt phase and do not read it as disloyalty.
Have leadership commit first: list the unknowns, assess worst cases, research what can be researched, such as a small pilot.
Bring others in through small groups with non-assumptive questions, listening without judging.
Ask for a directed response: answer now, give a timeline, or say 'I don't know'.
Let teammates propose the tasks that follow.

test.method: Check for a voiced doubt that was answered, and watch for people saying yes but not following through.
test.measure: other:change_adoption_rate
test.read_point: 4 to 6 weeks after the rollout starts

title: Use the 30-item team culture scale only as a discussion prompt, never as a measurement
hypothesis: If the 30-item team culture scale is run only as a conversation starter, with its inconsistent score bands stated openly, and the 15-statement dysfunction assessment stays the primary instrument, then the team avoids treating an internally contradictory scale as a real measurement, because the source itself states both 'below 60' and 'below 25' as the low-score threshold without reconciling them.
does_not_apply_when: only 1 team instrument will be run at all, in which case use the 15-statement assessment instead

signal.check: The team culture scale's total score is being reported as a definitive measurement rather than a discussion prompt.

expected_effect.size: unknown; 1 source, internally inconsistent bands

risk.note: A framing choice for how results are presented.

steps: Administer the 30 items on a 0 to 4 scale.
Total the first 25 items, max 100, and compute the odd and even sums and their gap.
Score items 25 to 30 as the leadership sub-score, max 24.
State openly that the source's own bands are inconsistent (below 60 and below 25 both called low).
Use the results only to start a conversation, never to rank teams or replace the primary assessment.

test.method: Not a split test; a framing and disclosure check.
test.measure: whether the inconsistency was stated when results were shared
test.read_point: Each time the scale is used

title: Run a native genius interview and give the strength public credit
hypothesis: If a leader asks a team member 3 rounds of why past a surface skill to find what they do easily and without being asked, then names that strength back to them and gives it a visible role, then the person takes on more of that work with less prompting, because naming raises their own awareness and confidence in it.

signal.check: A team member's real strength has never been named out loud, or the same 2 people always get handed the interesting work by default.

expected_effect.size: no number given; the source claims the practice raises confidence and use of the strength, not a percent

risk.note: The interview and the naming cost only time; the risk is a shallow answer that mislabels the strength.

steps: Pick 1 team member whose real strength has not been explicitly named.
Ask what they do better than anyone around them, without effort and without being asked or paid.
Push past the first surface answer by asking why 3 times.
Name the strength back to them in plain words.
Connect the named strength to a real, visible task or decision.
Check in a month later whether they took on more of that work unprompted.

test.method: Compare how often the person volunteers for that kind of work before and after the naming conversation.
test.measure: Frequency of unprompted contribution in that specific strength area

title: Use a fixed talk-time budget to stop 1 voice from dominating meetings
hypothesis: If every person in a meeting gets a fixed number of talk turns or a time budget, then a founder or loud specialist stops filling the whole room, because the device forces restraint without needing a confrontation.

signal.check: The same 1 or 2 people speak in most of a meeting, and quieter members rarely offer an idea unprompted.

expected_effect.size: no number given; the source frames it as a facilitation device, not a measured lift

risk.note: Cheap to try for 1 meeting; the risk is it feels gimmicky if not explained first.

steps: Pick a recurring meeting where 1 or 2 people talk most of the time.
Give every attendee a fixed number of talk tokens or a shared time budget for the session.
Explain the reason before starting, not mid-meeting.
Run the meeting and let people spend their own budget.
Note who spoke and for how long afterward.
Repeat for 3 to 4 sessions and compare the spread of participation.

test.method: Track speaking time or turn count per attendee across sessions with and without the device.
test.measure: Spread of speaking time across attendees
test.read_point: After 3 to 4 sessions using the device

title: Label leadership comments as soft or hard so casual remarks do not become policy
hypothesis: If a leader states out loud whether a comment is a soft opinion, food for thought, or a hard directive, then the team stops treating offhand remarks as new rules, because the label removes the guesswork about how much weight to give it.

signal.check: Team members quietly change plans or priorities after an offhand leader comment that was never meant as a directive.

expected_effect.size: no number given; the source offers it as a verbal convention, not a measured result

risk.note: Costs nothing to adopt; the risk is the leader forgetting to label a comment and it gets read as a directive anyway.

steps: Before making a comment on someone's work or plan, decide if it is food for thought or a real directive.
State the label out loud: soft opinion or hard opinion.
Ask the team to flag back if an unlabelled comment is being treated as a rule.
Review after a month whether any soft comments turned into unintended changes.

test.method: Ask the team periodically whether an unlabelled comment was ever treated as a rule change.
test.measure: Count of offhand comments mistaken for directives
test.read_point: 1 month after adopting the labelling habit

title: Ask for a fast rough answer before deciding to invest more time in a plan
hypothesis: If a leader asks for a quick, partial answer within a short window instead of demanding a full plan or giving no guidance at all, then the team tests direction cheaply before committing real time, because a rough pass surfaces the wrong assumptions early.

signal.check: A brief or plan is either handed over fully formed or left completely open ended, with no cheap checkpoint in between.

expected_effect.size: no number given; the source's own example uses a 2-day rough pass before committing weeks to a full answer

risk.note: Cheap and reversible; the main risk is treating the rough pass as final and skipping the deeper work it was meant to earn.

steps: Pick a task or brief that would normally get either a full spec or no direction at all.
Ask the owner for a rough, partial answer within 1 to 2 days.
Review the rough answer together and decide whether it earns more time.
Only then commit to the fuller version, with a new deadline.

test.method: Compare time spent on a rejected full plan under the old approach versus a rough-pass-first approach.
test.measure: Hours spent before a wrong direction is caught
test.read_point: Next time a plan or brief is assigned

title: Pair a stretched owner with an active backup instead of taking ownership away
hypothesis: If a person stretched into a bigger role gets a second person as an active backup and sounding board, then the stretch succeeds without the original owner losing accountability, because the backup adds capacity without taking the decision away.

signal.check: A stretched owner is either left alone to sink or swim, or the leader quietly takes the task back at the first sign of trouble.

expected_effect.size: no number given; the source's own case is 1 illustrative pairing, not a measured rate

risk.note: Costs a second person's time; the risk is the backup quietly taking over instead of staying support.

steps: Identify an owner who has been stretched into a role above their current comfort.
Name a second person as an explicit backup and sounding board, not a co-owner.
State plainly that the original owner keeps the decision and the accountability.
Check in with both people after the first milestone to confirm the split is holding.

test.method: Track whether the original owner still makes the final call and whether the project stays on track with the backup in place.
test.measure: Whether ownership stayed with the original person and the milestone was hit

title: Require a proposed fix alongside every problem someone escalates
hypothesis: If nobody is allowed to hand up a flagged problem without also proposing a fix, then the team stops offloading half-finished thinking onto the leader, because the rule forces the escalation to include a next step, not just a complaint.

signal.check: People bring the leader problems with no proposed next step, and the leader ends up doing the thinking that was the escalator's job.

expected_effect.size: no number given; the source states this as a personal rule the author enforces, not a measured result

risk.note: Costs nothing to state; the risk is people under-escalating a real problem to avoid the extra step.

steps: State the rule to the team: no flagged problem without a proposed fix attached.
The next time someone escalates a bare problem, ask them to come back with a proposed fix first.
Accept a rough or wrong proposed fix rather than none at all.
Watch for under-escalation and explicitly invite bare flags on anything genuinely urgent.

test.method: Track the share of escalations that arrive with a proposed fix attached over a month.
test.measure: Share of escalations with a fix attached

title: Let people face the natural consequence of a missed deadline instead of rescuing them
hypothesis: If a leader lets a missed deadline or a bad call play out to its natural consequence instead of quietly fixing it, then the person takes the next deadline more seriously, because rescuing signals they are not trusted to handle it and lowers effort next time.

signal.check: A leader routinely reworks a missed deliverable at the last minute or smooths over the fallout rather than letting the owner face it.

expected_effect.size: no number given; the source offers this as a leadership principle, not a measured lift

risk.note: Low cost to apply; the risk is a real customer or revenue cost if the consequence is severe, so reserve it for internal, recoverable misses.

prerequisites: A miss that is safe to let play out, not one that risks a customer or a large loss.
steps: Identify a missed internal deadline or a bad call that is safe to let play out.
Resist stepping in to quietly fix it before the consequence lands.
Let the owner experience the fallout, then debrief what they will do differently.
Reserve rescuing for misses that would cause real customer or revenue harm.

test.method: Compare on-time rates for that owner's deliverables before and after letting 1 consequence play out.
test.measure: On-time delivery rate for the affected owner
test.read_point: Next 2 to 3 deliverables from that owner

title: Run a quarterly check on how much capability your management is actually getting
hypothesis: If each key person privately estimates what percent of their full capability their manager is actually getting from them, then a leader finds an underutilisation gap before adding headcount, because a low self-reported percentage points at a management fix, not a staffing one.

signal.check: Nobody has ever asked the team, even privately, what share of their real capability current management is drawing out.

expected_effect.size: the source's own interview data spans 20 to 50 percent under weak management versus 70 to 100 percent plus under strong management, self-reported and not measured

risk.note: A private, low-stakes question; the risk is people giving a socially safe answer instead of an honest one.

steps: Privately ask each key person what percent of their full capability their manager gets from them.
Ask the same question about a past manager for comparison.
Treat any answer in the 40 to 60 percent range or below as a signal to fix before hiring.
Repeat the question each quarter and track the trend, not just 1 reading.

test.method: Compare the self-reported percentage across quarters for the same people.
test.measure: Self-reported percent of capability extracted

title: Check after a hard meeting whether the room gave safe answers or real ones
hypothesis: If a leader asks after a tough meeting whether people held back with safe, agreeable ideas or offered bold, risk-taking ones, then a fear-driven climate gets caught early, because a pattern of only-safe answers is a concrete signal, not a mood read.

signal.check: A meeting on a hard topic produced quick agreement with little visible pushback or new ideas.

expected_effect.size: no number given; the source frames it as a qualitative after-meeting check, not a measured score

risk.note: Costs a few minutes of reflection; the risk is the leader misreading genuine agreement as a bad sign.

steps: After a hard meeting, ask whether the ideas offered were safe and agreeable or bold and risky.
Ask 1 or 2 attendees privately whether they held anything back.
If safe-only answers repeat across meetings, treat it as a climate problem to fix, not a one-off.
Track the pattern across the next few hard meetings.

test.method: Track how often hard meetings produce only safe, agreeable ideas versus real pushback over a run of meetings.
test.measure: Share of hard meetings with visible pushback or new ideas
test.read_point: Over the next 3 to 5 hard meetings

title: Track whether a returned problem gets solved by you again or handed back to its owner
hypothesis: If a leader watches whether a delegated problem that resurfaces gets solved by the leader again or handed back to the owner with a question, then micromanagement gets caught as a pattern, because doing the actual thinking on delegated work is the concrete tell, not a feeling.

signal.check: A delegated problem comes back to the leader more than once and the leader ends up doing the thinking on it.

expected_effect.size: no number given; the source frames this as a self-diagnostic, not a measured rate

risk.note: No direct cost; the risk is the leader not noticing the pattern without deliberately tracking it.

steps: For the next 2 weeks, note every delegated problem that comes back to you.
For each one, record whether you solved it yourself or handed it back with a question.
If you are solving most of them yourself, name that as the pattern in your own review.
Practice handing 1 back with a question the next time it happens.

test.method: Track the ratio of self-solved versus handed-back returns over 2 weeks.
test.measure: Share of returned problems handed back to the owner

title: Avoid engaging with a person or project only when it becomes visible to leadership
hypothesis: If a leader keeps an even level of involvement in a project instead of jumping in only when it becomes visible to senior leadership, then the team stops experiencing an unpredictable bungee boss, because inconsistent engagement produces both dependency and disengagement.

signal.check: A leader is fully engaged in a project only when it is about to be seen by someone senior, and absent otherwise.

expected_effect.size: no number given; the source names this as a named Micromanager pattern, not a measured result

risk.note: No direct cost; the risk is the leader not noticing their own visibility-driven pattern without feedback.

steps: Ask a trusted peer or report whether your involvement in a project tracks its visibility to leadership.
If it does, set a fixed, lower-effort check-in cadence instead of visibility-triggered spikes.
Hold that cadence even when nobody senior is watching.
Ask again in a month whether the pattern has changed.

test.method: Ask the team directly whether your engagement in a project still spikes around visible moments.
test.measure: Reported consistency of leader involvement
test.read_point: 1 month after setting a fixed cadence

title: Hold people accountable to their best effort, not to an outcome outside their control
hypothesis: If a leader demands people's best effort and execution rather than a specific outcome they cannot fully control, then pressure produces engagement instead of stress, because demanding an uncontrollable outcome punishes people for factors outside their reach.

signal.check: A team member is judged on an outcome (a sale, a rating) that depends heavily on factors they do not control, rather than on the effort and execution they do control.

expected_effect.size: no number given; the source frames this as a distinction between pressure and stress, not a measured result

risk.note: No direct cost; the risk is conflating this with lowering standards, when the standard is on effort and execution, not the bar itself.

steps: Before a review, separate what the person controls from what they do not for the outcome in question.
Set the accountability conversation around effort and execution on the controllable parts.
State plainly what part of the result was outside their control.
Hold the same standard for yourself when your own results depend on others.

test.method: Ask affected team members whether they feel judged on effort or on outcomes outside their control.
test.measure: Reported clarity on what they are held accountable for

title: Run the Personal Histories icebreaker before asking a new team for hard trust work
hypothesis: If a team runs a 30-minute round robin of simple biographical questions before doing harder trust work, then the group gets visibly warmer and looser fast, because a short, low-risk shared disclosure lowers the barrier to the harder exercises that follow.

signal.check: A team is about to do harder trust or conflict work together and has never done a simple shared disclosure exercise first.

expected_effect.size: the source describes a team as visibly tighter after about 45 minutes than at any point in the prior year, a single illustrative case, not a controlled result

risk.note: Costs 30 minutes of meeting time; the risk is treating the short lift as lasting without following with real work.

steps: Set aside at least 30 minutes in a meeting or offsite.
Go round the table with the same short list of low-sensitivity questions: siblings, hometown, a childhood challenge, first job.
Have the leader go first, including the leader, so status differences flatten.
Move into substantive work while the group is still loose, since the effect fades once real work resumes.
Note anyone who does not participate or gets excluded from the warmth, as a signal to watch.

test.method: Observe team warmth and openness in the meeting immediately after the exercise versus a typical meeting.
test.measure: Qualitative team warmth in the following work session
test.read_point: Same meeting, immediately after the exercise

title: Run the Team Effectiveness Exercise: 1 contribution and 1 improvement per peer
hypothesis: If every team member privately names 1 top contribution and 1 needed improvement for each peer, then reports it to that person one at a time starting with the leader, then real development areas surface that a generic review misses, because peer input is more specific than a manager's alone.

signal.check: The team has some baseline trust but has never given each other direct, specific peer feedback on contribution and improvement.

expected_effect.size: no number given; the source's own claim is that 60 minutes is usually enough for a full team pass

risk.note: Higher-risk than a simple icebreaker since it surfaces real criticism; skip it if the team has no baseline trust yet.

prerequisites: The team has already done a lower-risk trust exercise, such as Personal Histories.
steps: Ask each member to privately write, for every peer, their single biggest contribution and the one thing to improve.
Report responses 1 person at a time, with peers giving input while that person listens without defending.
Start with the team leader so the leader is the first evaluated.
Budget at least 60 minutes for a full team pass.
Follow up on each named development area in later 1-on-1s so it is not a one-off event.

test.method: Track whether named development areas show visible change in the following month's 1-on-1s.
test.measure: Progress on named development areas
test.read_point: 1 month after the exercise, in follow-up 1-on-1s

title: Run a 5-minute strength and weakness round tied to team impact, leader first
hypothesis: If each person writes their single biggest strength and weakness framed as their impact on the team's success or failure, with the leader going first and generic or falsely modest answers banned, then real staffing decisions follow, because named gaps become explicit assignments or coaching plans instead of vague self-talk.

signal.check: A team has never named individual strengths and weaknesses in terms of concrete team impact, only in generic personality terms.

expected_effect.size: no number given; the source frames this as a low-risk vulnerability exercise, not a measured lift

risk.note: Low cost; the risk is a shallow or defensive answer, which the source says should not be forced deeper in the moment.

steps: Give each person 5 minutes to write their single biggest strength and weakness, framed as impact on team success or failure.
Ban a generic weakness and false modesty about a real strength.
Have the leader go first to model the standard.
Let peers sharpen a shallow or off-target answer rather than letting it stand.
Turn each named gap into a real staffing decision, coaching plan, or assignment.

test.method: Check whether named gaps turned into an actual assignment, coaching plan, or hire within the following month.
test.measure: Share of named gaps acted on

title: Interrupt a retreating debate to say the discomfort is expected, then confirm it helped
hypothesis: If a facilitator briefly interrupts when the team visibly pulls back from a needed debate to say the discomfort is necessary and expected, then afterward confirms the conflict helped, then the team stays in a hard discussion instead of retreating to false agreement, because naming the discomfort in the moment gives people permission to keep going.

signal.check: A team visibly backs away from a hard but necessary debate the moment it gets uncomfortable.

expected_effect.size: no number given; the source names this a facilitation move, not a measured result

risk.note: No direct cost; the risk is over-using the interruption and making every disagreement feel forced.

steps: Watch for a debate visibly retreating into agreement or silence right when it gets hard.
Interrupt briefly to say the discomfort is expected and needed.
Let the debate continue rather than moving on.
After the decision, confirm out loud that the conflict was good for the team.

test.method: Track how often a debate reaches a real decision versus retreats to premature agreement, before and after using the move.
test.measure: Share of hard debates reaching a real decision

title: Give each team member a conflict-style read and choose a mode on purpose
hypothesis: If each team member learns their own default conflict style, such as competing, avoiding, compromising, accommodating or collaborating, then the team chooses a mode deliberately for a given decision, because a default habit is not always the right fit for the stakes of that specific call.

signal.check: The team has never discussed default conflict styles and always handles disagreement the same way regardless of the decision's stakes.

expected_effect.size: no number given; the source names the tool as a way to choose a mode deliberately, not a measured result

risk.note: Needs a licensed instrument or a lighter self-assessment substitute; check current licensing before committing budget.

steps: Have each team member complete a conflict-style assessment, or a lighter self-rating against the 5 named styles.
Share results as a team discussion, not a permanent label.
Before a high-stakes disagreement, name which mode the team will deliberately use.
Review after the decision whether the chosen mode fit the stakes.

test.method: Ask the team after a high-stakes decision whether the deliberately chosen conflict mode fit the situation.
test.measure: Reported fit of the chosen conflict mode to the decision
test.read_point: Next high-stakes decision after the assessment

title: Ask in review whether resources moved mid-period to save a goal in jeopardy
hypothesis: If a regular review meeting asks out loud how often the team moved budget, stock or people between areas mid-period to save a goal that was in jeopardy, then a team that never reallocates gets caught before the goal fails, because a 'never' answer is a concrete fear-of-conflict or complacency signal.

signal.check: A goal was missed and nobody can point to a moment mid-period when resources were actually moved to try to save it.

expected_effect.size: no number given; the source's own illustrative case answers 'never' to this question

risk.note: No direct cost; the risk is asking the question without acting on a 'never' answer.

steps: Add the question to the review agenda: how often did we move resources mid-period to save a goal in jeopardy?
Ask it out loud in the meeting, not as a written survey.
If the answer is 'never' or 'rarely,' treat it as a signal, not just an answer.
Name 1 resource-reallocation option the team could have used and did not.

test.method: Track the answer to this question across consecutive review meetings.
test.measure: Reported count of mid-period reallocations

title: Set 2 meeting ground rules and defend them against pushback
hypothesis: If a leader sets 2 simple ground rules, be present and participate, no laptops or phones, and holds the line when someone calls it unrealistic for the industry, then meetings get more real engagement, because a stated and defended norm changes behaviour more than an unstated expectation.

signal.check: Meetings routinely have people on devices or visibly checked out, and no explicit ground rule has ever been set.

expected_effect.size: no number given; the source presents this as 1 leader's illustrative case, not a measured result

risk.note: No direct cost; the risk is the rule being dropped the first time it is challenged.

steps: State 2 simple ground rules for the next recurring meeting: be present, participate, no devices.
Explain why before the first meeting under the new rule.
When someone objects that it is not realistic for the team's pace or industry, hold the line.
Check after a few meetings whether engagement visibly changed.

test.method: Compare visible engagement (side conversations, device use, contribution) before and after the rule.
test.measure: Qualitative meeting engagement
test.read_point: After 3 to 4 meetings under the new rule

title: Defend the time cost of a planning or team session against 'this is not real work'
hypothesis: If a leader defends the time booked for a planning or team-health session when someone calls it a distraction from real work, then the session actually happens instead of being the first thing cut, because an unprotected time investment is the easiest thing for a busy team to sacrifice.

signal.check: A planning offsite, quarterly review, or team-health session is at risk of being cancelled because someone calls it less urgent than daily tasks.

expected_effect.size: no number given; the source presents this as a leadership stance to hold, not a measured result

risk.note: No direct cost; the risk is defending a session that genuinely should be cut for a real emergency, so use judgement on true urgency.

steps: Before the session, expect at least 1 objection that it is not real work.
State plainly why the investment matters for the decisions the team is stuck on.
Hold the time unless a genuine emergency displaces it.
Run the session and note whether the objection resurfaces next time.

test.method: Track how often planning or team sessions get held versus cancelled over a year.
test.measure: Share of scheduled sessions actually held
test.read_point: Over the next year of scheduled sessions

title: Run a dedicated debrief on how the team feels after a deserved departure
